parole.significato: pain, suffering
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin -algia. By surface analysis, alg- + -ia.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a tail-like structure.
parole.testo: From New Latin cercus, from Ancient Greek κέρκος (kérkos, “tail”).

parole.significato: shinned
parole.testo: From New Latin cnēmis, from Ancient Greek κνήμη (knḗmē, “shin”) + -ic.

parole.significato: any spherical microorganism
parole.testo: From New Latin coccus, from Latin coccum, from Ancient Greek κόκκος (kókkos, “grain, seed”).

parole.significato: Denoting diseases characterized by inflammation, itself often caused by an infection.

parole.significato: Word.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek ὄνυμα (ónuma), Doric and Aeolic dialectal form of ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”); compare also -onymy § Etymology.

parole.significato: functional disease or condition such as hepatosis
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin -ōsis, from Ancient Greek -ωσις (-ōsis, “state, abnormal condition, or action”), from -όω (-óō) stem verbs + -σις (-sis).

parole.significato: Synonym of -phasia: forms names of speech disorders.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin -phēmia, from Ancient Greek φήμη (phḗmē, “voice”).

parole.significato: Used to form nouns meaning fear of a specific thing.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin, from Ancient Greek -φοβία (-phobía), from φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: Bearer, carrier or conveyor.
parole.testo: From New Latin -phorus, from Ancient Greek -φόρος (-phóros, “bearing”), a derivative of φέρω (phérō, “to bear, to carry”). See phoresy.

parole.significato: Growth or formation
parole.testo: From New Latin -plasia, from Ancient Greek πλάσις (plásis, “molding, formation”).

parole.significato: rupture
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ῥῆξις (rhêxis), from ῥήγνυμι (rhḗgnumi).

parole.significato: Tone, condition.
parole.testo: From New Latin -tonia, from Ancient Greek -τονία (-tonía) (in ἀτονία (atonía)), from τόνος (tónos) + -ία (-ía). Compare French -tonie, German -tonie.

parole.significato: Having a trema (hole or aperture) or tremata of the type, position or number specified by the prefix.
parole.testo: From New Latin trēma (“aperture”), from Ancient Greek τρῆμα (trêma), from Proto-Hellenic *trḗmə (“hole”), from Proto-Indo-European *tréh₁-mn̥ (“to drill”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to drill”).

parole.significato: urine; urination; presence in urine (of a substance denoted by a prefixed combining form); state or condition of the ur…
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, Latin -ūria, from Ancient Greek -ουρία (-ouría), from οὖρον (oûron, “urine”).

parole.significato: From time immemorial; from an infinitely remote point in the past.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ab aeternō.

parole.significato: From inconvenience or hardship.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ab inconvenientī.

parole.significato: from inside; from within
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ab intrā (“from within”).

parole.significato: One of the tiles or squares of a tessellated pavement; an abaculus.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀβακίσκος (abakískos, “a coloured stone for laying mosaic”), diminutive of ἄβαξ (ábax, “board”). See abacus.

parole.significato: An inability to walk due to a defect in muscular coordination.
parole.testo: From New Latin a- (“without”) + Ancient Greek βάσις (básis, “step”) + New Latin -ia (“pathological condition”).

parole.significato: An abbot who is exempt from diocesan control, and acts with papal authority.
parole.testo: Partly translated from New Latin abbas nullius, short for abbas nullius dioecesis (“abbot of no diocese”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the abdomen; ventral.
parole.testo: First attested in 1746. From New Latin abdōminālis, from Latin abdōmen. Equivalent to abdomin- + -al. Compare French abdominal.

parole.significato: abdomen; abdominal.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Latin abdomen, which see.

parole.significato: Each of the sixth pair of cranial nerves that are the motor nerves supplying the lateral rectus in the eye.
parole.testo: From New Latin nervus abdūcēns (“nerve leading away”).

parole.significato: Relating to an abductor
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin abductōrius.

parole.significato: The edible and aromatic seed pods (properly, capsules) of the Abelmoschus moschatus.
parole.testo: From New Latin abelmoschus, from Arabic حَبّ الْمِسْك (ḥabb al-misk, “pills of musk”).

parole.significato: A typically malignant fatty tumor located on the trunk.
parole.testo: Named after John Abernethy, English surgeon, + New Latin, from Ancient Greek σάρκωμα (sárkōma, “fleshy growth”), from σαρκόω (sarkóō, “become fleshy”), from σάρξ (sárx, “flesh”).

parole.significato: The fourth digestive compartment of the stomach of a cow or other ruminant, after the omasum;
parole.testo: From New Latin abomāsum, from ab- (“away from”) + omāsum (“tripe of a bullock”).

parole.significato: An abortion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin abortus (“miscarriage”). Doublet of abort.

parole.significato: An order of annelids, so called because the species composing it have no special organs of respiration, usually includi…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + βράγχια (bránkhia, “gills”) + -ata.

parole.significato: Either of the ratlike rodents that form the genus Abrocoma; rat chinchilla.
parole.testo: From New Latin abrocoma, from Ancient Greek ἁβροκόμης (habrokómēs, “with delicate hair”), from ἁβρός (habrós, “splendid, delicate”) + κόμη (kómē, “hair”).

parole.significato: A premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin abruptiō placentae (literally “a breaking off of the placenta”).

parole.significato: The defendant being absent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin absente reō.

parole.significato: Without impeachment of waste, i.e. without accountability for waste, without legal liability for waste.
parole.testo: From New Latin.

parole.significato: Absence of willpower or decisiveness, especially as a symptom of mental illness.
parole.testo: From New Latin abūlia, from Ancient Greek ἀβουλία (aboulía, “irresolution”), from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + βουλή (boulḗ, “will”).

parole.significato: Any of the various tropical flowering plants of the genus Abutilon, such as the flowering maple, Indian mallow, or Chin…
parole.testo: From New Latin [Term?], from Arabic أَبُو طِيلُون (ʔabū ṭīlūn, “Indian mallow”).

parole.significato: The garden in Athens where the academics met.
parole.testo: From New Latin academia, from Ancient Greek Ἀκαδημία (Akadēmía); Doublet of academia, academy, and Akademeia. parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin acadēmīa, from Ancient Greek Ἀκαδημία (Akadēmía), a grove of trees and gymnasium outside of Athens where Plato taught; from the name of the supposed former owner of that estate, the Attica hero Akademos. parole.significato: Having thorns.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἄκανθος (ákanthos, “thorn plant”), from ἄκανθα (ákantha, “thorn”).

parole.significato: A point lying near the base of the nose; specifically, the point at the base of the anterior nasal spine that lies on t…
parole.testo: From New Latin acanthion, from Ancient Greek ἄκανθα (ákantha, “thorn”) + -ion.

parole.significato: With thorns
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἄκανθος (ákanthos, “thorn plant”), from ἄκανθα (ákantha, “thorn”).

parole.significato: Any fish of the superorder Acanthopterygii.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from acanthus (“thorn”), (from Ancient Greek ἄκανθος (ákanthos)) + Ancient Greek πτερύγιον (pterúgion) diminutive of πτέρυξ (ptérux, “wing, fin”), from πτερόν (pterón, “feather, wing”).

parole.significato: The spindle-shaped embryo stage of Acanthocephala that burrows into the body cavity of its first intermediate host.
parole.testo: From New Latin acanthus (“spine”) (extracted from taxonomic name Acanthocephala) + -or (condition).

parole.significato: The state in which the level of carbon dioxide in the blood and tissue is significantly lower than normal.
parole.testo: From New Latin acapnia, from Ancient Greek ἄκαπνος (ákapnos, “without smoke”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + καπνός (kapnós, “smoke”).

parole.significato: Any parasitic arachnid, such as mites and ticks, of the subclass Acarina.

parole.significato: mite

parole.significato: An extinct rhinoceros of the genus †Aceratherium.
parole.testo: From New Latin †Aceratherium.

parole.significato: Shaped like a saucer or shallow cup.
parole.testo: From New Latin acetabuliformis, from acetabulum (“saucer”) + -form.

parole.significato: cup-shaped; acetabular.
parole.testo: From New Latin acetabulosus; by surface analysis, acetabulo- + -ous.

parole.significato: The strong tendon formed of the united tendons of the large muscles in the calf of the leg, and inserted into the bone…
parole.testo: Calque of New Latin tendo Achillis, in reference to the mythological account of Achilles being held by the heel when dipped in the River Styx. Its coinage has been attributed to Dutch anatomist Philip Verheyden in 1693, but the term is first attested in 1684.

parole.significato: Deficiency or absence of bile.
parole.testo: From New Latin acholia, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + χολή (kholḗ, “bile”).

parole.significato: Lactobacillus acidophilus, one of the bacteria commonly used in fermenting yogurt
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin acidophilus (“acid-loving”).

parole.significato: Shaped like a scimitar.
parole.testo: From New Latin acīnacifōrmis, from acinaces (“short sword”) + -form.

parole.significato: A skin condition, usually of the face, that is common in adolescents. It is characterised by red pimples, and is caused…
parole.testo: From New Latin acnē, probably a corruption of Ancient Greek ἀκμή (akmḗ, “point, top”).

parole.significato: Synonym of rosacea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin acnē rosācea (literally “rose-colored acne”), from its resemblance to acne, which it is no longer considered as such.

parole.significato: Threadlike defensive organs, composed largely of nettling cells (cnidae), thrown out of the mouth or special pores of c…
parole.testo: From the plural of New Latin acontium, from Ancient Greek ἀκόντιον (akóntion, “little dart”).

parole.significato: Partial or total absence of the skull.
parole.testo: From New Latin acrania, from a- + crānium + -ia.

parole.significato: The extremities: limbs, head, fingers, toes, etc.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, per above.

parole.significato: A lack or defect of the pulse.
parole.testo: From New Latin acrotismus, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, privative a) + κρότος (krótos, “a rattling, beating”) + -ismus.

parole.significato: Radiation; emission or projection.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin actinobolismus, from Koine Greek ἀκτινοβόλος (aktinobólos, “emission of rays”) + -ismus. Ἀκτινοβόλος is from ἀκτίς (aktís, “ray”) + βόλος (bólos, “a throw”). First attested in the 1650s.

parole.significato: The insertion of needles into the (living) tissue of the body affecting the Qi or energy along energetic pathways of th…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin acūpūnctūra, from Latin acus + pūnctūra. First attested in 1684. By surface analysis, acu- + puncture.

parole.significato: For a particular purpose.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin ad hoc (“to this, for this”).

parole.significato: At pleasure.
parole.testo: Abbreviation of ad libitum, borrowed from New Latin ad libitum.

parole.significato: An insect of the genus Adelges.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Adelges + -id, first attested in 1928. The Latin term is adapted from a purported Ancient Greek *ἀδελγεῖν (*adelgeîn, “to suck”), which is unattested; it is likely there was some confusion with ἀμελγεῖν (amelgeîn, “to milk, to suck up moisture, to drink”). parole.significato: A cutaneous disorder consisting of angiofibromas that begin in childhood (generally present between 2–5 years of age) a…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin adenōma sēbāceum.

parole.significato: Literary works not attributed to (or claimed by) an author. (Originally used as a title of collections of anonymous Gre…

parole.significato: Defective perspiration; adiaphoresis.
parole.testo: From New Latin adiapneustia, from Ancient Greek ἀδιαπνευστία (adiapneustía, “lack of perspiration”).

parole.significato: Containing, composed of, or consisting of fat; fatty.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, from New Latin adipōsus, from Latin adeps (“fat, lard”). By surface analysis, adip- + -ose; Latin adeps (“fat, lard”) is probably related to Umbrian 𐌀𐌛𐌄𐌐𐌄𐌔 (ařepes, “offerings of fat”) since 𐌛 (ř) in Umbrian regularly represents an earlier *d.

parole.significato: adiposity; obesity
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin adipōsitās.

parole.significato: A female administrator.
parole.testo: From New Latin administrātrīx. By surface analysis, administrator + -trix.

parole.significato: A work of adoxography.
parole.testo: From New Latin adoxus (“absurd, paradoxical”) from Ancient Greek ἄδοξος (ádoxos, “obscure, ignoble”) (from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + δόξα (dóxa, “expectation”)) + -graph.

parole.significato: Fine writing on a minor or trivial subject.
parole.testo: From New Latin adoxus (“absurd, paradoxical”) (from Ancient Greek ἄδοξος (ádoxos, “obscure, ignoble”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + δόξα (dóxa, “expectation”)) + -γραφίᾱ (-graphíā, “writing”).

parole.significato: A copulatory organ of some male insects.
parole.testo: From New Latin aedeagus, derived from Ancient Greek αἰδοῖα (aidoîa, “private parts, pudenda”) + ἀγός (agós, “leader”), from ἄγω (ágō, “I lead”).

parole.significato: The failure of a mother (human or otherwise) to produce sufficient milk following birth.
parole.testo: From New Latin agalactia, from Ancient Greek ἀγαλακτία (agalaktía, “lack of milk”), from ἀγάλακτος (agálaktos) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from ᾰ̓- (ă-, “not; without”) + γᾰ́λᾰ, γᾰ́λᾰκτος (gắlă, gắlăktos, “milk”).

parole.significato: A mass, assemblage, or sum of particulars; something consisting of elements but considered as a whole.
parole.testo: From Middle English aggregat(e) (“a sum, unit, complex, aggregate”), borrowed from New Latin aggregātum (“an aggregate”), substantivized from the nominative neuter singular of aggregātus, the perfect passive participle of aggregō (“to flock together”), from ad- (“at, to, toward”)) + gregō (“to flock

parole.significato: Grouped together.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin agminātus, from the Classical Latin agmen (“a troop”, oblique stem: agmin-) + -ātus (“-ate”). Compare the Latin agminātim (“in hosts”, “in hordes”, adverb).

parole.significato: Any grass of the genus Agrostis of bentgrasses.
parole.testo: From New Latin agrōstis, via the genus name taxonomic name Agrostis.

parole.significato: Any of several deciduous Asiatic trees of the genus Ailanthus, including the tree of heaven.
parole.testo: From New Latin Ailanthus, from Ambonese Malay ai lanto (“tree (of) heaven”).

parole.significato: Any member of the family Ailuridae.
parole.testo: From New Latin Ailuridae, as Ailurus + -id.

parole.significato: Any member of the subfamily Ailurinae.
parole.testo: From New Latin Ailurinae (“taxonomic subfamily”), as Ailurus + -ine.

parole.significato: Having white flowers.
parole.testo: From New Latin albiflōrus (“white-flowered”).

parole.significato: A chronic disease caused by compulsive and uncontrollable consumption of alcoholic beverages, leading to addiction and…
parole.testo: From alcohol + -ism. Derived from New Latin alcoholismus chronicus, coined by the Swedish professor of medicine Magnus Huss in 1849.

parole.significato: A certain color morph of the black rat, once regarded as a distinct subspecies.
parole.testo: From its original habitat; a calque of New Latin rattus alexandrīnus.

parole.significato: A preservative against infectious diseases.
parole.testo: From New Latin alexitericum, from neuter of alexitericus (although apparently first attested later); see Etymology 2.

parole.significato: Resisting poison or venom.
parole.testo: From New Latin alexitericus, from alexiterium + Classical Latin -icus; see alexitery.

parole.significato: An antidote to poison.
parole.testo: From New Latin alexiterium and its etymon Ancient Greek ἀλεξητήριον (alexētḗrion, “remedy”), from neuter of ἀλεξητήριος (alexētḗrios, “keeping off, defending”), from ἀλεξητήρ (alexētḗr, “defender, protector”) + -ιος (-ios, adjectival suffix), from extended stem of ἀλέξω (aléxō, “to ward off”) + ‑τήρ

parole.significato: Acting as an antidote to poison.
parole.testo: From New Latin alexiterius, from Ancient Greek ἀλεξητήριος (alexētḗrios, “keeping off, defending”); see Etymology 1.

parole.significato: The repetition of consonant sounds or letters at the beginning of two or more words immediately succeeding each other,…
parole.testo: From New Latin allīterātiō, from allīterātus, from allīterō, from Latin ad (“to, towards, near”) and lītera (“a letter”).

parole.significato: of a different nature or kind.
parole.testo: From New Latin, based on Ancient Greek. By surface analysis, allo- + gen- + -eous.

parole.significato: A plant of the species Aloe vera, grown as an ornamental, thought to have medicinal value; an extract, often a gel, mad…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin aloē vēra (“true aloe”).

parole.significato: A compound purgative medicine of which aloes is a chief ingredient.
parole.testo: From New Latin aloēdarium, from Ancient Greek ἀλοηδάριον (aloēdárion), from ἀλόη (alóē, “aloes”).

parole.significato: alphabetic; rudimentary
parole.testo: From New Latin alphabetarius, from Late Latin alphabētum. See alphabet.

parole.significato: Helpless at birth (of young animals); or having young which are helpless at birth.
parole.testo: From New Latin Altrices (a former division of birds), plural of altrīx, the feminine of altor (“nourisher”), from alere (“to nourish”).

parole.significato: American, Canadian, and Philippines standard spelling of aluminium.
parole.testo: Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1812, after the earlier 1807 New Latin form alumium. By surface analysis, Latin alumen + -um

parole.significato: A bony ridge or raised thickened border of the upper or lower jaw that contains the sockets of the teeth.
parole.testo: From New Latin processus alveolaris (“protuberance of tooth sockets”).

parole.significato: Any form of blindness that is accompanied by no obvious change to the eye; often the result of disease of the optic ner…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin amaurōsis, from Ancient Greek ἀμαύρωσις (amaúrōsis, “dimming, obscuring, amaurosis”), from ᾰ̓μαυρόω (ămauróō, “to grow dim”), from ἀμαυρός (amaurós, “dim”).

parole.significato: Dimness or blurring of the eyesight due to a fault in transmission of signals to the brain from an otherwise healthy ey…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin amblyōpia. By surface analysis, ambly- + -ope + -ia.

parole.significato: of, relating to, or suffering from amblyopia
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin amblyōpicus. By surface analysis, ambly- + -ope + -ic.

parole.significato: The formation of tooth enamel
parole.testo: From New Latin amelogenesis. By surface analysis, amelo- + -genesis.

parole.significato: Absence of menstrual discharge.
parole.testo: Via New Latin from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + μήν (mḗn, “month”) + -ροια (-roia, “flowing”). By surface analysis, a- + meno- + -rrhoea.

parole.significato: The bowfin, Amia calva.
parole.testo: From New Latin amia.

parole.significato: The univalent NH₄⁺ cation, derived by the protonation of ammonia
parole.testo: From New Latin ammōnium. Equivalent to ammonia + -ium.

parole.significato: A small scale-like leaf on the underside of stems of certain liverworts.
parole.testo: From New Latin amphi- (“near”) + gastr- (“belly; ventral”) + -ium. Attested from the 19th century.

parole.significato: Having lobes (usually auriculate) that completely surround the stem.
parole.testo: From New Latin amplexicaulis.

parole.significato: starch
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Latin amylum (whence English amylum, amyl, and amyl-/amylo-).

parole.significato: A member of a radical wing of Christians during the Protestant Reformation, with a tenet of adult baptism.
parole.testo: From New Latin anabaptista, from the Ancient Greek ἀναβαπτισμός (anabaptismós), itself from ἀνα- (ana-, “re-”) and βαπτισμός (baptismós, “baptism”), equivalent to ana- + Baptist.

parole.significato: To baptize or christen again, or to a different denomination; to rename or rechristen
parole.testo: From New Latin anabaptizāre, from Ancient Greek ἀνα- (ana-, “again”) + βᾰπτῐ́ζω (băptĭ́zō, “to baptize”). See baptize and Anabaptist.

parole.significato: A chronological mistake; the erroneous dating of an event, circumstance, or object.
parole.testo: From New Latin anachronismus, from Ancient Greek ἀναχρονισμός (anakhronismós), from ἀναχρονίζομαι (anakhronízomai, “referring to the wrong time”), from ἀνά (aná, “up against”) + χρονίζω (khronízō, “spending time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). Analyzable as ana- + chrono- + -ism.

parole.significato: To refer to, or put into, a wrong time period.
parole.testo: From anachronism + -ize. From New Latin anachronismus, from Ancient Greek ἀναχρονισμός (anakhronismós), from ἀναχρονίζομαι (anakhronízomai, “referring to the wrong time”), from ἀνά (aná, “up against”) + χρονίζω (khronízō, “spending time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”).

parole.significato: An unstressed syllable at the start of a verse.

parole.significato: The inability to feel pain.

parole.significato: An aecium of some rust fungi that has no peridium or outer membrane.
parole.testo: New Latin caeoma, from Ancient Greek καίειν (kaíein, “to burn”) + -ωμα (-ōma). Attested from 1832.

parole.significato: The combination of state (originally imperial) power with religious authority; state authority over ecclesiastical matt…
parole.testo: From caesar + -o- + papism, probably modelled after New Latin caesaro-papia, coined by the German ecclesiastical jurist Justus Henning Böhmer (1674–1749) in his work Jus ecclesiasticum Protestantium (Ecclesiastical Law of the Protestants, 1714–1736).

parole.significato: Synonym of calcifugal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin calcifugus (“limestone-phobic”). By surface analysis, calci- + -fugous.

parole.significato: Bearing or producing calluses.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin callifer, equivalent to callus + -i- + -ferous.

parole.significato: Either of two rounded lobes at the posterior base of the wing in many true flies.
parole.testo: From New Latin calyptra, from Ancient Greek κᾰλύπτρα (kălúptra, “hood”), from κᾰλύπτω (kălúptō, “I cover”).

parole.significato: A darkened chamber in which the image of an outside object is projected and focused onto a surface.
parole.testo: From New Latin camera obscūra (literally “dark chamber”); compare camera.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Luís de Camões.
parole.testo: From New Latin Camoniānus [from Camonius + -ānus] or directly from Portuguese Camon- (stem of Camões) + -ian.

parole.significato: Shaped like a bell.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin campānulātus, from campānula (“litte bell”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A mass of sterile fibers within a fruiting body interspersed among spores.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin, “hair (collectively)”, from capillus.

parole.significato: Having a very small knob-like termination, or collected into minute capitula.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin capitellātus, from capitellum + -ātus, diminutive of caput (“head”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Any of various tropical American plants, of the genus Capsicum, principally the species Capsicum annuum and Capsicum fr…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin capsicum, from Ancient Greek καψικός (kapsikós, “like a box”), from Latin capsa (“box”).

parole.significato: A carpal, especially one of the series articulating with the metacarpals.
parole.testo: From New Latin ōs carpāle, from Ancient Greek καρπός (karpós, “wrist”).

parole.significato: Synonym of carpel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin carpellum. See carpel for more.

parole.significato: The group of bones that make up the wrist.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin carpus, from Ancient Greek καρπός (karpós, “wrist”).

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to, Descartes, his mathematical methods, or his philosophy, especially with regard to its emphasis on…
parole.testo: From the New Latin Cartesiānus, from Cartesius (“René Descartes”).

parole.significato: The female menstrual discharge.
parole.testo: From New Latin catamenia, from Ancient Greek καταμήνια (katamḗnia), the neuter plural of καταμήνιος (katamḗnios, “monthly”), from κατά (katá) + μήν (mḗn, “month”). First attested in 1750.

parole.significato: A severe psychiatric condition, often associated with schizophrenia, characterized by a tendency to remain in a rigid s…
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, from German Katatonie, from New Latin catatonia, from a Greek word meaning to stretch tight. By surface analysis, cata- + tone + -ia.

parole.significato: Purgative; inducing mental or physical catharsis.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin catharticus, from Ancient Greek καθαρτικός (kathartikós).

parole.significato: A disorder with intense burning pain, type 2 of two types of complex regional pain syndrome.
parole.testo: From New Latin causalgia, from Ancient Greek καῦσος (kaûsos, “burning heat”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”). By surface analysis, caus- + -algia.

parole.significato: A small (50–100 nanometer) invagination of the plasma membrane in many vertebrate cell types.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin caveola, constructed from cavea (“hollow, cavity; cage”) + -ola (diminutive suffix). Doublet of jail, which is from Late Latin caveola, an earlier, natural formation of the same term. More at cave, cavum, cava and cage.

parole.significato: Chronic joint pain, especially of the hip-joint.
parole.testo: From New Latin cedmata, from the Ancient Greek κέδματα (kédmata).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, consisting of, or resembling a cell or cells.
parole.testo: From New Latin cellulāris, from cellula (“cell”) + -āris.

parole.significato: An inflammation of subcutaneous or connective tissue caused by a bacterial infection.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin cellulitis. By surface analysis, cellule + -itis. Doublet of cellulite. First attested in the 1840s.

parole.significato: The Swiss pine, Pinus cembra.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin cembra.

parole.significato: The central, or one of the central, bones of the carpus or tarsus in most vertebrates. In the human tarsus it is repres…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin centrāle.

parole.significato: Tending, or causing, to recede from the center.
parole.testo: From New Latin centrifugālis, coined by Christiaan Huygens from Latin centrum (“center”) + fugiō (“to flee”) + -al.

parole.significato: Directed or moving towards a centre.
parole.testo: From New Latin centripetālis coined by Sir Isaac Newton, from Latin centrum (“center”) + petō (“to seek, aim”) + -al. Analysable as centri- + -petal.

parole.significato: A dorsal or lateral outgrowth on the body of nudibranchs.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek κέρας (kéras, “horn”).

parole.significato: The parasitic larva of trematodes that infect the final host generally.
parole.testo: From New Latin cercāria, from Ancient Greek κέρκος (kérkos, “tail”) + -āria.

parole.significato: A structure on the end of the abdomen of most insects, sometimes long, hairlike sensory organs and sometimes smaller an…
parole.testo: From New Latin cercus, from Ancient Greek κέρκος (kérkos, “tail”).

parole.significato: A parasitic flatworm of the class Cestoda; a tapeworm.
parole.testo: From New Latin Cestoda, from cestus (“girdle, belt”), from Ancient Greek κεστός (kestós, “of Aphrodite’s charmed girdle”).

parole.significato: Copper; relatedly, also bronze or brass.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek χαλκός (khalkós, “copper”). Despite the appearance in English of a possible relation of chalco- to chalk, and any plausible semantic and cognate connections between limestones and ores in ancient times, the terms are not related by any known cognation. parole.significato: Synonym of jungle cat (Felis chaus)
parole.testo: From New Latin chaus, from a native, probably Turkic, name; compare Nogai кавыс (kavıs).

parole.significato: The corner of the mouth (as used in cephalometry)
parole.testo: From New Latin, equivalent to cheilo- (“lip”) + -ion (“cephalometric reference point”).

parole.significato: The typical pentadactyloid limb of the higher vertebrates.
parole.testo: From New Latin cheiropterygium, from Ancient Greek χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + πτερύγιον (pterúgion, “wing, fin”).

parole.significato: Either of the prehensile claws found on the proboscis of chelicerates (horseshoe crabs, sea spiders and arachnids).
parole.testo: From New Latin chēlicera, from Ancient Greek χηλή (khēlḗ, “jawbone”) + κέρας (kéras, “horn”).

parole.significato: Practising chemistry (or, earlier, alchemy); pertaining to these sciences.
parole.testo: From New Latin chemicus, chimicus, chymicus.

parole.significato: Relating to or using chemicals or chemistry.
parole.testo: Back-formation from compounds built on New Latin chēmicus (“pertaining to alchemy or chemistry”) and chēmia (“chemistry”), ultimately of Ancient Greek origin.

parole.significato: A crossing of two nerves, ligaments etc.
parole.testo: From New Latin chiasma, from Ancient Greek χῑ́ασμα (khī́asma), from χῑάζω (khīázō, “to mark with an X”).

parole.significato: A Chinese pink (Dianthus chinensis).
parole.testo: From New Latin chinensis + -y.

parole.significato: snow
parole.testo: From New Latin chion- (“snow”), chio, German chio, from Ancient Greek χιών (khiṓn, “snow”), χιόνι (khióni, “snow”), akin to Ancient Greek χειμών (kheimṓn, “winter”).

parole.significato: inflammation of the eyes caused by exposure to ultraviolet light
parole.testo: From New Latin chionablepsia. By surface analysis, chion- (“snow”) + ablepsia (“blindness”).

parole.significato: massage as a form of therapy
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek χειραψίᾱ (kheirapsíā, “massage”), from χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + ἅψις (hápsis, “contact, touching”), from ἅπτω (háptō, “to touch”).

parole.significato: hand
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin chiro-.

parole.significato: Any of various rock-clinging marine molluscs of the class Polyplacophora, including the genus Chiton.
parole.testo: ] From New Latin chiton. See above.

parole.significato: Any of several common, often asymptomatic, sexually transmitted diseases caused by the microorganism Chlamydia trachoma…
parole.testo: From New Latin chlamydia, from Ancient Greek χλαμύδιον (khlamúdion, “small cloak”), from χλαμύς (khlamús, “cloak”).

parole.significato: A funnel; a funnel-shaped opening.
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin choana, from Ancient Greek χοᾰ́νη (khoắnē, “funnel”), from χέω (khéō, “to pour”) + -ᾰ́νη (-ắnē, suffix for utensil names).

parole.significato: A condition caused by the presence of excess bile in the blood, sometimes leading to somnolence and coma.
parole.testo: From New Latin cholaemia, from Ancient Greek χολή (kholḗ, “gall, bile”) + αἷμα (haîma, “blood”). By surface analysis, chole- + -aemia.

parole.significato: Relating to the common bile duct.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from New Latin choledochus, from Ancient Greek χοληδόχος (kholēdókhos, “bile-containing”).

parole.significato: A branch of the facial nerve that traverses the middle ear cavity and the infratemporal fossa and supplies autonomic fi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin chorda tympanī (“cord of the tympanum”).

parole.significato: The cord-like tendons that connect the papillary muscles to the tricuspid valve and the mitral valve in the heart.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin chordae tendineae (literally “tendinous (tendon-like) cords”), from Latin chordae (plural of chorda (“cord, rope”)) + New Latin tendineae (plural of tendinea (“tendinous”), from Medieval Latin tendō (“tendon”)).

parole.significato: Relating to chorography.
parole.testo: From New Latin chōrographicus, from Ancient Greek χωρογραφικός (khōrographikós). By surface analysis, choro- + -graphic.

parole.significato: Resembling the chorion, particularly in containing many blood vessels.
parole.testo: From New Latin choroides, from Ancient Greek χοροειδής (khoroeidḗs, alteration of χοριοειδής (khorioeidḗs, “like the afterbirth”)), from χόριον (khórion, “membrane that encloses the fetus in the womb, afterbirth”) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-like”).

parole.significato: A collection of written passages, used to learn an unfamiliar language.
parole.testo: From New Latin chrēstomathia, from Ancient Greek χρηστομάθεια (khrēstomátheia, “desire for learning; book containing a summary of useful knowledge or select passages,”).

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol Cr) with an atomic number of 24: a steely-grey, lustrous, hard and brittle transition metal.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from French chrome (from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”)) + -ium. So called because of the striking colors of its compounds.

parole.significato: The science of determining the order in which events occurred.
parole.testo: From chrono- (“relating to time”) + -logy (“study of, account of”), after New Latin chronologia from Ancient Greek χρόνος (khrónos, “time”) + λόγος (lógos, “reason, explanation”). Literally "time reason" in Modern Greek.

parole.significato: Ciliated, having cilia.
parole.testo: First attested in 1760; borrowed from New Latin ciliātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A tree or shrub of the genus Cinchona, native to the Andes in South America but since widely cultivated in Indonesia an…
parole.testo: From New Latin cinchona, from Spanish Chinchón. Named by Carl Linnaeus after Ana de Osorio, 4th Countess of Chinchón (1599–1625), the wife of the Spanish Viceroy of Peru, who was allegedly cured of a fever by the bark.

parole.significato: film, movie, cinema (moving pictures).
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek κῑνέω (kīnéō, “to move”). Compare kine-.

parole.significato: Characteristic of spiders of the species Loxosceles rufescens (syn. Loxosceles citigrada).
parole.testo: New Latin citigradus (“moving swiftly”), from citus and gradior, equivalent to Latin citus + -i- + -grade.

parole.significato: A flattened organ arising from the stem of a plant, often replacing the leaves in photosynthetic function, as leaves in…
parole.testo: From New Latin cladodium, from Ancient Greek κλᾰ́δος (klắdos, “young slip of a tree”).

parole.significato: A branch of a ramose spicule, which collectively form the cladome.
parole.testo: From a New Latin form of Ancient Greek κλάδος (kládos, “branch”). Doublet of clade and possibly holt.

parole.significato: Resembling a club, becoming increasingly wide from the base to the distal end.
parole.testo: First attested in 1661; borrowed from New Latin clāvātus, from Latin clāva (“club”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, clav(a) + -ate.

parole.significato: Minutely clavate; shaped like a little club.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin clāvellātus, from clāvella (diminutive of clāva (“club”)) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: An early form of harpsichord.
parole.testo: From New Latin clāvicymbalum.

parole.significato: A glandular swelling in the epidermis of some annelid worms; it secretes a viscous fluid in which the eggs are deposite…
parole.testo: From New Latin clitellum, from Latin clītella (singular noun), clītellae (“packsaddle”, plurale tantum).

parole.significato: Synonym of clitellum.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin clitella, clitellae (“packsaddle”).

parole.significato: A sensitive elongated erectile sex organ at the anterior part of the vulva in female humans and other mammals.
parole.testo: From post-classical New Latin clītoris (16th century), from Koine Greek κλειτορίς (kleitorís), probably from Ancient Greek κλείω (kleíō, “to sheathe, shut”), in reference to it being covered by the labia minora. The related noun form κλείς (kleís) has a second meaning of "a key, a latch or hook (to

parole.significato: The section of the leg from the knee to the ankle; shin.
parole.testo: From New Latin cnēmis, from Ancient Greek κνήμη (knḗmē, “shin”).

parole.significato: A nematocyst.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek κνίδη (knídē, “stinging nettle; anemone”).

parole.significato: Any of various invertebrate animals, such as jellyfish, hydras, sea anemones, corals and formerly sponges and ctenophor…
parole.testo: From translingual Cnidaria + -an, derived from New Latin Cnīdāria, derived from Ancient Greek κνῑ́δη (knī́dē, “sea nettle”).

parole.significato: A mass formed by means of coagulation.
parole.testo: From New Latin coāgulātum, substantivized from the nominative neuter singular of coāgulātus, see -ate (noun-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

parole.significato: Any approximately spherical bacterium.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin coccum, from Ancient Greek κόκκος (kókkos, “grain, seed”).

parole.significato: Any of the class Actinistia of primitive lobe-finned fish in the order Coelacanthiformes—thought to have been extinct f…
parole.testo: From the New Latin genus name Coelacanthus, from Ancient Greek κοῖλος (koîlos, “hollow”) + ἄκανθα (ákantha, “spine”), referring to the hollow caudal fin rays of the first fossil specimen described and named by Louis Agassiz in 1839.

parole.significato: Any simple aquatic animal formerly considered to belong to the phylum Coelenterata, now divided into the cnidarians and…
parole.testo: From scientific New Latin Coelenterata.

parole.significato: A prehensile-tailed tree-dwelling porcupine, of genus Coendou, found in Central and South America.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Old Tupi kûandu.

parole.significato: A parasitic infestation of Taenia tapeworm larvae; most common in ungulates and canids
parole.testo: From New Latin coenurus + -osis.

parole.significato: A complex tapeworm larva growing interstitially in vertebrate tissues and consisting of a large fluid-filled sac from t…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek κοινός (koinós, “common”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”) + -ος (-os, nominal suffix).

parole.significato: To treat a material with a boiling liquid and repeatedly return the distillate.
parole.testo: From New Latin cohobātus, past participle of cohobāre, perhaps from Arabic كَعَّبَ (kaʕʕaba).

parole.significato: An East Asian grass (Coix lacryma-jobi), sometimes harvested as a cereal.
parole.testo: From New Latin coix, from Ancient Greek κόϊξ (kóïx, “doum palm”).

parole.significato: Synonym of mouthwash.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin collūtōrium, from collūtum, supine of colluere (“to wash thoroughly”).

parole.significato: Openings for ventilation in Ancient Roman aqueducts.
parole.testo: From New Latin colluviarium, from Latin colluviēs (“filth, dregs”) + -arium.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the colon.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Latin colon, whence also English colon.

parole.significato: Any bird of either of the genera Colius or Urocolius, endemic to sub-Saharan Africa.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin Colius.

parole.significato: Serving to commemorate something.
parole.testo: First attested in 1612; borrowed from New Latin commemorātīvus, from commemorō. By surface analysis, commemorate + -ive, cognate with French commémoratif.

parole.significato: Pertaining to commemoration.
parole.testo: First attested in 1695; borrowed from New Latin commemorātōrius, from Latin commemorō. Cognate with French commémoratoire, by surface analysis, commemorate + -ory.

parole.significato: A fraction in the form of one integer divided by another, non-zero, integer.
parole.testo: Originally a calque of New Latin fractiō vulgāris. See vulgar fraction.

parole.significato: The state of being compatible; in which two or more things are able to exist or work together in combination without pr…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin compatibilitās. By surface analysis, compatible + -ity.

parole.significato: To penetrate every part of (something); to permeate.
parole.testo: First attested in 1636; borrowed from New Latin compenetrātus, perfect passive participle of compenetrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, con- + penetrate.

parole.significato: A device that produces pressure, such as a gas compressor that produces pressurized gas.
parole.testo: From compress + -or, or from New Latin compressor.

parole.significato: The act, process or ability of concentrating; the process of becoming concentrated, or the state of being concentrated.
parole.testo: From New Latin concentrātiō (“(1550) action or an act of coming together at a single place; (1659) extraction or separation of one or more of the metals present in an alloy”). parole.significato: To come together at a common centre.
parole.testo: (late 16th century) From a Romance language, see French concentrer, Italian concentràre, Spanish concentrar; alternatively from Medieval Latin/New Latin concentrō. By surface analysis, con- + centre. Doublet of concentrate.

parole.significato: To inflect (a verb) for each person, in order, for one or more tenses; to list or recite its principal parts.
parole.testo: The adjective (as “combined, united”) and noun are first attested in 1471, in Middle English, the verb in 1530; partly from Middle English conjugat(e) (“combined, united”), partly directly borrowed from New Latin coniugātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin coniugō (“to yoke together, combine

parole.significato: Agreement about the terms and subject matter of a contract between all involved parties.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin consensus ad idem (“agreement to the same thing”). In English, first attested in 1864.

parole.significato: Total deafness.
parole.testo: From New Latin cōphōsis, from Ancient Greek κώφωσις (kṓphōsis).

parole.significato: A change in structure and function of the right ventricle of the heart as a result of a respiratory disorder.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin cor pulmōnāle (literally “pulmonary heart”).

parole.significato: Any of several composite herbs, of genus Coreopsis, typically with bright yellow flowers.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek κόρις (kóris, “bedbug”) + New Latin -opsis (“resembling in appearance”), from Ancient Greek ὄψις (ópsis, “aspect, appearance”).

parole.significato: Having a crest or a crownlike appendage, a corona.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin coronātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Coronilla of plants related to the clover, having their flowers arranged in little heads or tufts rese…
parole.testo: From New Latin coronilla, from Latin corona (“crown”) + Spanish -illa.

parole.significato: One of the pair of cylindrical columns of erectile tissue that form the bulk of the clitoris and penis.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin corpus cavernōsum (“body full of hollows or cavities”).

parole.significato: The evidence that a crime has occurred.
parole.testo: From New Latin corpus dēlictī (literally “body of the crime”).

parole.significato: The mass of spongy erectile tissue surrounding the urethra within the penis or clitoris.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin corpus spongiōsum (“spongy body”).

parole.significato: A thin stratum of involuntary muscular fiber that radiates from the anus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin corrūgātor cutis ānī (“wrinkler of the skin of the anus”).

parole.significato: A small narrow pyramidal muscle at the medial end of the eyebrow.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin corrūgātor superciliī (“wrinkler of the eyebrow”).

parole.significato: Synonym of cosine.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin cosinus, abbreviation of complementi sinus. Doublet of cosine.

parole.significato: Finely ribbed or costate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin costellātus, from costella (“small rib”) + -ātus, from costa (“rib”) + -ella (forms diminutives), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A Belgian variety of whetstone, containing spessartine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin cōticula, from cōtis (“whetstone”) + -cula (“diminutive suffix”).

parole.significato: Any of the neotropical passerine birds of the family Cotingidae.
parole.testo: From New Latin cotinga, from Old Tupi cutinga.

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Crepis in the family Compositae.
parole.testo: From New Latin crēpis, from Ancient Greek κρηπίς (krēpís, “crepida; foundation”). Doublet of crepida.

parole.significato: Having a cribellum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin cribellatus or from cribellum + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the cricoid and arytenoid cartilages.
parole.testo: From crico- + arytenoid, or borrowed from New Latin cricoarytaenoīdēs.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or being a cricoid cartilage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin cricoīdēs, from Ancient Greek κρῐκοειδής (krĭkoeidḗs, “ring-shaped, annular”), from κρίκος (kríkos, “ring”) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-like, -oid”).

parole.significato: A standard, test, or requirement by which individual things or people may be compared and judged; a gauge.
parole.testo: From New Latin criterion, from Ancient Greek κριτήριον (kritḗrion, “a test, a means of judging”), from κριτής (kritḗs, “judge”), from κρίνω (krínō, “to judge”); see critic.

parole.significato: Any of various plants, of the genus Croton, that yield croton oil.
parole.testo: From New Latin crotōn, from Ancient Greek κροτών (krotṓn, “tick”), from the size and shape of the seed.

parole.significato: With a grain of salt; with a bit of common sense and skepticism.
parole.testo: A New Latin coinage, derived from the phrase cum grānō salis (which was not used in Classical Latin).

parole.significato: Without deliberation or hesitation: extempore, off-the-cuff.
parole.testo: From New Latin currente calamō (“with the pen running on”).

parole.significato: The interval of a planet's orbit in which its curtate or shortened distance is less than the true distance.
parole.testo: First attested in 1584; borrowed from New Latin curtātiō, from curtō + -tiō.

parole.significato: Any arboreal marsupial of most genera of the family Phalangeridae, native to northern Australia, New Guinea, and Indone…
parole.testo: From New Latin Cuscus, former genus name, ultimately (probably via French and Dutch koeskoes) from a local word for the marsupials in a language of the Moluccas.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, existing on, or affecting the exterior skin, especially the cutis.
parole.testo: From New Latin cutaneus, from Latin cutis (“skin”).

parole.significato: Synonym of damnatio memoriae.

parole.significato: Having downy leaves.

parole.significato: Having ten points or teeth.
parole.testo: From New Latin decemdentātus. By surface analysis, decem- + dentate.

parole.significato: The making of ten identical copies of something.

parole.significato: Tapering to a blunt end.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin dēcollātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

parole.significato: To eject or throw (someone or something) from or through a window.

parole.significato: The act of throwing something or especially someone out of a window, especially lethally.
parole.testo: From New Latin defenestratio, from dē (“from; out”) + fenestra (“window”) + -atio (suffix indicating an action or process); compare Middle French défenestrer (modern French défenestrer), défenestration, Italian defenestrazione and German Fenstersturz. parole.significato: Opening of an organ by its own means (such as an anther or a seed pod) to release its contents.
parole.testo: From New Latin dehiscentia (in Linnaeus), from Latin dehiscentem, present participle of dehiscō. By surface analysis, dehisce + -ence.

parole.significato: destroyer.
parole.testo: From New Latin dēlētērius, from Ancient Greek δηλητήρῐος (dēlētḗrĭos). Doublet of deleterious.

parole.significato: The triangular space under the beak of many brachiopod shells.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin deltidium. By surface analysis, delta + -idium.

parole.significato: A small muscle of each side of the upper lip that is inserted into the nasal septum and wing of the nose on each side a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin dēpressor sēptī nāsī (“depressor of the septum of the nose”).

parole.significato: The inner layer of the skin.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin derma, from Ancient Greek δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”). Doublet of derm.

parole.significato: Inflammation of the skin.
parole.testo: From New Latin dermatītis, from δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”), from δέρω (dérō, “to skin, flay”). By surface analysis, dermato- + -itis.

parole.significato: The tissue of the skin underlying the epidermis.
parole.testo: From New Latin dermis, from Ancient Greek δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”), from δέρω (dérō, “to skin, to flay”).

parole.significato: dermal: dermis, but also often, broadly, skin or epidermis.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek δέρμα (dérma, “skin”); compare dermis § Etymology.

parole.significato: A climbing leguminous plant of Southeast Asia and the southwest Pacific Islands, Derris elliptica, whose roots are a so…
parole.testo: From New Latin and translingual Derris, from Ancient Greek δέρρις (dérrhis, “leather, skin”), referring to the leathery pods, from δέρω (dérō, “I skin, I flay”).

parole.significato: A vessel used in alchemy to extract and filter oils.
parole.testo: From New Latin descensorium. Compare Old French descensoire. See descend.

parole.significato: A medical disorder commonly called diabetes, characterized by varying or persistent hyperglycemia (high blood sugar lev…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin diabetes mellitus (“diabetes of the sweet type”) (from the fact that in centuries past, physicians sometimes tasted a patient's urine to help diagnose the illness).

parole.significato: A figure of speech in which multiple arguments are brought to bear on a single point.
parole.testo: From New Latin diallagē, from Ancient Greek διαλλαγή (diallagḗ, “interchange”).

parole.significato: The migration of blood cells, especially leucocytes, through the intact walls of blood vessels into the surrounding tis…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek, from dia- + Ancient Greek πηδᾰ́ω (pēdắō, “I leap”).

parole.significato: A separation between two parts, such as separation of a bone, without fracture.
parole.testo: From New Latin diastasis, from Ancient Greek διάστασις (diástasis, “separation, standing aloof”), from δια- (dia-) + στάσις (stásis, “standing”). Compare diastema.

parole.significato: A hereditary or constitutional predisposition to a disease or other disorder.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin diathesis, from Ancient Greek διάθεσις (diáthesis, “state, condition”), from διατίθημι (diatíthēmi, “to arrange”).

parole.significato: A cymose inflorescence with all branches below the terminal flower in regular opposite pairs.
parole.testo: From New Latin dichasium, from di- + Ancient Greek χάσις (khásis, “chasm, separation”).

parole.significato: Any spider in the family Dictynidae.
parole.testo: Originally only capitalized, from New Latin Dictynidae (“taxonomic family”), as Dictyna + -id.

parole.significato: The region of the human brain, specifically the human forebrain, that includes the thalamus, the hypothalamus, the epit…
parole.testo: From New Latin diencephalon, from di-, prevocalic form of dia- + encephalon.

parole.significato: To modify so as to create a difference or distinction.
parole.testo: From New Latin differentiātus, perfect passive participle of differentiō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from Latin differentia (“difference”); see difference.

parole.significato: The bending of a wave around an obstacle.
parole.testo: From New Latin diffrāctiō (in which coined by Francesco Maria Grimaldi), from Latin diffrāctus, past participle of Latin diffringo (“to shatter, to break into pieces”). Coined in Physico-mathesis de lumine (1665) by Francesco Maria Grimaldi.

parole.significato: Having two bellies.
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin digastricus, from di- (“twice, doubly”) + gastricus (“gastric”); equivalent to di- + gastric. Doublet of digastricus.

parole.significato: Synonym of digastric muscle.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin digastricus, ellipsis of mūsculus digastricus (“digastric muscle”). Doublet of digastric.

parole.significato: double
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek διπλόος (diplóos), διπλοῦς (diploûs, “double”).

parole.significato: Excessive production of urine; polyuria.
parole.testo: From New Latin diūrēsis, from Ancient Greek διουρέω (diouréō, “to urinate”) + -σις (-sis). Morphologically, δῐουρέω (dĭouréō) can be analysed as δι- (di-) + οὐρέω (ouréō).

parole.significato: Synonym of divergence.
parole.testo: From New Latin divergentia; by surface analysis, diverge + -ency.

parole.significato: A classical historian who describes the opinions of Ancient Greek philosophers and scientists.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin doxographus, itself coined by German classicist Hermann Diels in 1879 from Ancient Greek δόξα (dóxa, “opinion, belief”) + -γράφος (-gráphos, “writer”), originally in reference specifically to the tradition stemming from Theophrastus, + -er. parole.significato: Any very small duct, typically lactiferous.
parole.testo: From New Latin ductulus, diminutive of Latin ductus. By surface analysis, duct + -ule.

parole.significato: difficult
parole.testo: From New Latin dys-, from Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-, “hard, difficult, bad”). Often confused with the separately derived prefix dis-.

parole.significato: Of or relating to, or causing degeneration or deterioration in offspring.
parole.testo: From dys- + -genic, produced from New Latin dys- from Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) and γένος (génos, “offspring”).

parole.significato: A disabling neurological disorder in which prolonged and repetitive contractions of muscles cause jerking, twisting mov…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin dystonia, from German Dystonie. By surface analysis, dys- + -tonia.

parole.significato: Used to prefix product names, to indicate an electrified or all-electric variant of the product, particularly cars.

parole.significato: Having no bracts.

parole.significato: Having no bracteoles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ebracteolatus.

parole.significato: A skin discoloration caused by bleeding underneath the skin, especially one that is remote from a site of trauma or cau…

parole.significato: A complication of pregnancy characterized by seizures and coma due to hypertension.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin eclampsia, from French éclampsie, from Ancient Greek ἔκλᾰμψῐς (éklămpsĭs, “sudden development, violent onset”, literally “brightness”), from ἐκλᾰ́μπω (eklắmpō, “to shine or beam forth; to burst forth violently”) + -σῐς (-sĭs, nominal suffix).

parole.significato: Having no ribs or nerves.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ecostatus, ecostata.

parole.significato: Not cribellate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ecribellatus, ecribellata; see cribellate.

parole.significato: A woman perceived to have a highly sensitive emotional state, or prone to quasi-mystical trances.
parole.testo: From New Latin ecstatica, from Ancient Greek ἐκστατικός (ekstatikós).

parole.significato: The condition where an organ or other body part has an abnormal position.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin ectopia, derived from Ancient Greek ἔκτοπος (éktopos, “away from a place”), from ἐκ- (ek-) + τόπος (tópos). By surface analysis, ec- + -topia.

parole.significato: An excessive accumulation of serum in tissue spaces or a body cavity.
parole.testo: From New Latin oedēma, from Ancient Greek οἴδημα (oídēma, “swelling”), from οἰδέω (oidéō, “I swell”).

parole.significato: Lacking teeth.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin edentatus.

parole.significato: The first printed edition of a work previously only published in manuscript form.
parole.testo: From New Latin ēditiō prīnceps (“first edition”), 1800s.

parole.significato: Capable of being educated.
parole.testo: From New Latin educabilis, from Latin ēducō (“to educate”) + -ābilis; see educate.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being effable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin effābilitās.

parole.significato: Having a definite (lobed) shape; not effuse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin effiguratus; compare figurate (figuratus).

parole.significato: Without glands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin eglandulōsus; see glandulose.

parole.significato: That lacks guttules at each end of the spore.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin eguttulatus, eguttulata; see guttulate.

parole.significato: elastic
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἐλᾰστός (elăstós, “ductile”).

parole.significato: Elasticity; especially the expansibility of a gas.
parole.testo: From New Latin elatēr, from Ancient Greek ἐλατήρ (elatḗr, “driver, that which drives away”).

parole.significato: The mineral wurtzilite.
parole.testo: From New Latin elatēr, from Ancient Greek ἐλατήρ (elatḗr, “driver, that which drives away”) + -ite.

parole.significato: A narrow piece separating the costa and corium in certain insects of the suborder Heteroptera.
parole.testo: From New Latin embolium, from Ancient Greek ἐμβόλιον (embólion, “insertion”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to an embryo.

parole.significato: The right of a government over the private property within its jurisdiction. Usually invoked to compel land owners to s…

parole.significato: Having a tendency to emulate others; imitative.
parole.testo: First attested in 1593; borrowed from New Latin emulatīvus, by surface analysis, emulate + -ive.

parole.significato: An ornament on a frieze or capital, consisting of festoons of fruit, flowers, leaves, etc.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἔγκαρπος (énkarpos, “containing fruit”) (ἐν- (en-) + καρπός (karpós)).

parole.significato: Commonwealth standard spelling of encyclopedia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin encyclopaedia; the English word is an etymologically restored spelling variant of earlier encyclopedia, q.v.

parole.significato: A process of bone formation in which ossification takes place within the substance of the cartilage.
parole.testo: From New Latin endostosis. By surface analysis, endo- + ostosis.

parole.significato: A fast or series of privations undertaken by the Cathars to purify the soul, often resulting in death.
parole.testo: From New Latin endūra, from Old Occitan endurar (“to fast, endure”).

parole.significato: Possessing or pertaining to energy.

parole.significato: sword-shaped
parole.testo: From New Latin ensatus, from Latin ensis (“sword”).

parole.significato: A salamander native to western North America in the genus Ensatina.
parole.testo: From New Latin Ensatina.

parole.significato: relating to the intestines.
parole.testo: From New Latin entero-, combining form from Ancient Greek ἔντερον (énteron, “intestine”).

parole.significato: The gut, the whole intestine (alimentary) canal
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἔντερον (énteron, “intestine”).

parole.significato: An extinct early Eocene mammal (Hyracotherium leporinum), ancestral to the modern horse.
parole.testo: Originally a genus name, Eohippus, formed in New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”). By surface analysis, eo- + Latin hippus.

parole.significato: the hindbrain.
parole.testo: From New Latin epencephalon, from ep- + encephalon.

parole.significato: Lasting for a short period of time.
parole.testo: From New Latin ephemerus, from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros), the more common form of ἐφημέριος (ephēmérios, “of, for, or during the day, living or lasting but for a day, short-lived, temporary”), from ἐπί (epí, “on”) + ἡμέρα (hēméra, “day”).

parole.significato: A journal or diary.
parole.testo: From New Latin ephēmeris, from Ancient Greek ἐφημερίς (ephēmerís, “diary, calendar”), from ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros, “daily”).

parole.significato: A projection, formed by a separate ossification, at the scapular end of the furcula of many birds
parole.testo: From New Latin, from epi- + Ancient Greek κλείς (kleís, “key, clavicle”) + -ium.

parole.significato: A cartilaginous organ in the throat of terrestrial vertebrates covering the glottis when swallowing to prevent food and…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin epiglōttis, from Ancient Greek ἐπῐγλωττῐ́ς (epĭglōttĭ́s, “valve covering the larynx”), from ἐπῐ- (epĭ-, “upon, over”) + γλωττῐ́ς (glōttĭ́s, “glottis, mouth of the windpipe”); equivalent to epi- (“upon; above”) + glottis.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an epigraph or to epigraphy.
parole.testo: From New Latin epigraphicus, from Ancient Greek ἐπῐγρᾰφῐκός (epĭgrăphĭkós). By surface analysis, epigraph + -ic.

parole.significato: The connective tissue framework and sheath of a nerve which bind together the nerve bundles, each of which has its own…
parole.testo: From New Latin epineurium, from Ancient Greek ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) + νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”).

parole.significato: A membranous tissue composed of one or more layers of cells which forms the covering of most internal and external surf…
parole.testo: From New Latin epithēlium. By surface analysis, epi- + thel- + -ium.

parole.significato: A horny excrescence on the top of the beak of some birds, notably the hornbill.
parole.testo: From New Latin epithema, from Ancient Greek ἐπίθεμα (epíthema, “lid, cover”).

parole.significato: A hard tumour or tumorous growth developed from the gums.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin epūlis.

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol Er) with atomic number 68: a silvery-white metal, in nature always found in combination with…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin erbium; itself from Swedish Ytterby (the name of the town where the element was discovered) + -ium. Coined by Swedish chemist and mineralogist Carl Gustaf Mosander in 1843. Doublet of terbium, ytterbium, and yttrium.

parole.significato: The group of muscles of the back responsible for erect posture of the vertebral column.
parole.testo: From New Latin.

parole.significato: A gradual decay through slow combustion or oxidation, like that of old trees or dead animals.
parole.testo: From New Latin ēremacausis, from Ancient Greek ἠρέμα (ēréma, “quietly”) + καῦσις (kaûsis, “burning”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the heath family (Ericaceae).
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin erīcāceus.

parole.significato: Interrogatory, proceeding by means of questions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin erōtēmaticus, from Koine Greek ἐρωτηματικός (erōtēmatikós, “interrogative; relating to questions”), from ἐρώτημα (erṓtēma, “question”) + -ικός (-ikós). Equivalent to obsolete erotema (“question”) + -tic.

parole.significato: Abnormal redness and inflammation of the skin, due to vasodilation.

parole.significato: of, or relating to the grammatical case that in some languages indicates existence in a state or capacity.
parole.testo: From New Latin casus essīvus (from Latin esse), coined in New Latin by Rasmus Rask.

parole.significato: A member of the eudicots.
parole.testo: Probably a back-formation from eudicots, short for eudicotyledons, from the New Latin coinage eudicotylēdōn, from the Ancient Greek components εὐ- (eu-, “good, well”) + δι- (di-, “two”) + κοτυληδών (kotulēdṓn, “cup-shaped cavity”); equivalent to eu- (“true”) + dicot.

parole.significato: An operation involving the removal of a part or parts of the body; excision, ectomy.
parole.testo: From New Latin exaeresis, from Ancient Greek ἐξαίρεσῐς (exaíresĭs, “a taking out, an extraction”).

parole.significato: A rash on the skin.
parole.testo: From New Latin exanthesis, from Ancient Greek ἐξάνθεσις (exánthesis). See exanthema.

parole.significato: Explanatory; serving to explain logically or in detail.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin explicātōrius, from Latin explicō (“to unfold, open out”). By surface analysis, explicate + -ory.

parole.significato: To drain (a living or dead body, or (medicine, surgery) a body part) of blood.
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₁ésh₂r̥ Learned borrowing from New Latin exsanguinātus (“depleted of blood, exsanguinated; lacking blood, bloodless”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Exsanguinātus is a participial adjective formed on ex- (“out, from”) + sanguī̆s (sanguin-) (“blood”) + -ātus.

parole.significato: One of the small sesamoid bones situated behind the condyles of the femur, in some mammals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin fābella, diminutive of Latin faba (“bean”).

parole.significato: Making; creative.
parole.testo: From New Latin factīvus, from Latin facere (“to make”).

parole.significato: The larger of the two folds of dura mater separating the hemispheres of the brain that lies between the cerebral hemisp…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin falx cerebrī (“the sickle of the brain”).

parole.significato: Erect and parallel.
parole.testo: From New Latin fastīgiātus (“peaked”) (from fastīgium), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Fatsia of Asian evergreen shrubs.
parole.testo: From the genus name, New Latin Fatsia.

parole.significato: Animals considered as a group; especially those of a particular country, region, time, biological group, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin fauna, from Latin Fauna, sister of Faunus (“god of forests and herdsmen”); akin to Ancient Greek θαῦνον (thaûnon, “wild animal, beast”), θώς (thṓs, “jackal, wild dog; panther”), Phrygian δάος (dáos, “wolf”).

parole.significato: Having cavities or cells like those of a honeycomb.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin faveolātus, from faveolus + -ātus, a diminutive of favus (“honeycomb”) modelled on alveolus; see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A South American evergreen shrub, Acca sellowiana (syn. Feijoa sellowiana).
parole.testo: From the New Latin former genus name Feijoa, which was named after Portuguese botanist João da Silva Feijó by the German botanist Otto Karl Berg.

parole.significato: The interstitial solid solution of carbon in body-centered cubic iron.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin ferrum (“iron”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Synonym of peroneus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin fībulāris, clipping of mūsculus fībulāris (“fibular muscle”).

parole.significato: Synonym of peroneus brevis.

parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin fībulāris longus, clipping of mūsculus fībulāris longus (“long fibular muscle”).

parole.significato: Synonym of peroneus tertius.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin fībulāris tertius, clipping of mūsculus fībulāris tertius (“third fibular muscle”).

parole.significato: Any of certain fishes of the genus Carapus.

parole.significato: The liquid or solution that has passed through a filter, and which has been separated from other fractions of the origi…
parole.testo: From the substantivation of New Latin filtrātus (“filtered”) past perfect participle of filtrō (“to filter”). Equivalent to filter (the verb) + -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Factious, tending to break into pieces.
parole.testo: An adaptation of New Latin fissiparus, from fissus (“split, cleft”) + pariō (“to bring forth”) by analogy with vīviparus.

parole.significato: Fan-shaped; having parts or segments that are flattened and lengthened on one side, such that they are long and narrow.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin flābellātus (“fanlike”). By surface analysis, flabell(um) (“fan-shaped structure”) + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The exocarp in citruses.
parole.testo: From New Latin flāvēdō (“yellowness, sallowness, yellow color”), derived from Latin flāvus (“yellow, golden”).

parole.significato: A muscle whose contraction acts to bend a joint or limb.

parole.significato: Belonging to, concerning, or located at a focus (definite location).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin focālis. By surface analysis, focus + -al.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to leaflets of a plant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin foliolātus, from foliolum (“leaflet”) + -ātus, a diminutive of folium (“leaf”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A shallow depression in the posterior dorsal midline of the tongue that is the remnant of the more cranial part of the…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin forāmen caecum (“an invisible, hidden opening”).

parole.significato: An aperture in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone that gives passage to the middle meningeal artery.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin forāmen spīnōsum (“thorny hole”).

parole.significato: Synonym of foraminifer (“any of a large group of aquatic amoeboid protists of the subphylum Foraminifera, characterized…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin Foraminifera (subphylum name), from French foraminifère (“foraminifer, foraminifera”), from French Foraminifères, coined by the French naturalist Alcide d’Orbigny (1802–1857) in an 1826 article. parole.significato: Synonym of form (“the component of a thing that determines its kind”).

parole.significato: Any of several shrubs, of the genus Forsythia, native to Asia and Eastern Europe, that are cultivated for their yellow…

parole.significato: Having small pits or depressions, like the receptacle in some composite flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin foveolātus (“pitted”), by surface analysis, foveola + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Yaws, the disease.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin frambēsia. Doublet of bramberry and framboise.

parole.significato: A small fold or ridge of tissue that supports or restrains the motion of the part to which it is attached, in particula…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin frēnulum, diminutive of frēnum (“a bridle, curb, bit”).

parole.significato: Any of several speech sounds produced by air flowing through a constriction in the oral cavity and typically producing…
parole.testo: From New Latin fricatīvus, from Latin fricāre (“to rub”).

parole.significato: To make cold or frigid.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin frīgēficō, frīgēficāre, causative of Classical frīgeō.

parole.significato: The time at which a plant unfolds its leaves.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin frondescentia, from frondescens, from Latin frondescō.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, directed toward, or situated at the front.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin frontālis, from frons (“the forehead, brow, front”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix), equivalent to front + -al; cognate of French frontal. Doublet of frontalis.

parole.significato: A muscle of the forehead, sometimes considered to be part of the occipitofrontalis muscle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin frontālis, clipping of mūsculus frontālis (“frontal muscle”). Doublet of frontal.

parole.significato: Imperfectly resembling a shrub.
parole.testo: About 1750, from New Latin frutēscēns.

parole.significato: Any alga of the genus Fucus.
parole.testo: From New Latin Fūcus, from Ancient Greek φῦκος (phûkos).

parole.significato: An offspring of a fundatrix.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from fundatri- (from fundātrīx) + -genia (irregular from Ancient Greek -γενής (-genḗs, “born”)).

parole.significato: Resembling or arranged in the form of a sling; specifically designating the lower part of the inferior constrictor musc…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin fundifōrmis (“shaped like a sling”), from funda (“a sling”) + -i- + -formis (“-form”).

parole.significato: A forked structure, a fork-like part.
parole.testo: From New Latin furca (“two-pronged fork”)

parole.significato: The rare earth gadolinium oxide
parole.testo: From New Latin gadolinia. See gadolinite.

parole.significato: Used to form medical and biochemical terms related to galactose
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek stem γάλακτ- (gálakt-) of γάλα (gála, “milk, milky sap, the Milky Way”).

parole.significato: Any of several species of trees of the genus Garcinia found in South and Southeastern Asia, especially Garcinia xanthoc…
parole.testo: From New Latin gambogium, cambogium (“resin from trees used to make yellow dye”), from New Latin Gambogia, Cambogia (“Cambodia”). The Latin word was first attested in English as a colour in 1634. Doublet of Cambodia and Kampuchea.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the stomach.
parole.testo: From New Latin gastricus, from Ancient Greek γαστήρ, γαστρός (gastḗr, gastrós, “stomach”). By surface analysis, gastr- + -ic; Doublet of gastrique.

parole.significato: The muscle at the back of the calf, whose insertion is the Achilles tendon at the heel.
parole.testo: 1670s, borrowed from New Latin gastrocnēmius, from Ancient Greek γαστροκνημία (gastroknēmía, “calf of the leg”), from γαστήρ (gastḗr, “paunch, belly”) + κνήμη (knḗmē, “leg”).

parole.significato: A flat, fan-shaped muscle that originates from the superior mental spine and inserts onto the undersurface of the tongu…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin genīoglōssus, clipping of musculus genīoglōssus (“genioglossal muscle”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the chin and hyoid bone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin genīohyoīdeus, clipping of musculus genīohyoīdeus; from Ancient Greek γένειον (géneion, “the chin”) + Latin hyoīdēs (“U-shaped”) + Latin -eus (adjectival suffix); equivalent to genio- (“relating to the chin”) + hyoid.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a genu or to the knee.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ǵónu From New Latin genuālis, from Latin genū (“knee”). By surface analysis, Latin genū + -al.

parole.significato: magistrates in Sparta who, with the kings, constituted the Gerousia
parole.testo: From New Latin Gerontes, from Ancient Greek γέροντες (gérontes, literally “elders”).

parole.significato: Relating to the gums.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin gingīvālis.

parole.significato: Of or written with the Glagolitic alphabet.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin glagoliticus, from Old Church Slavonic глаголица (glagolica), from глаголъ (glagolŭ, “word, speech”), Glagolitic spelling ⰳⰾⰰⰳⱁⰾⰻⱌⰰ (glagolica).

parole.significato: A conical vascularized body forming the extremity of the penis.
parole.testo: From New Latin glāns pēnis (“glans of the penis”), pēnis being a genitive.

parole.significato: The quality of being glaucescent, the state of being a bluish-green color.
parole.testo: By surface analysis, glaucescent + -ence, though Merriam-Webster presumes a New Latin *glaucēscentia, from New Latin glaucēscēns (“glaucescent”).
