parole.significato: Bearing, containing, or generating globules.
parole.testo: From globule + -iferous, after New Latin globulifera.

parole.significato: glomerulus
parole.testo: From glomerulus, from New Latin glomerulus, from glomus (“ball-shaped mass”) (stem glomer-) + -ulus (diminutive suffix). By surface analysis, glomerul- + -o-.

parole.significato: The opening between the true vocal cords which is located in the larynx and affects voice modulation through expansion…
parole.testo: Late 16th century borrowing from New Latin glōttis, from Ancient Greek γλωττῐ́ς (glōttĭ́s, “mouth of the windpipe”), from γλῶττᾰ (glôttă, “tongue”) + -ῐς (-ĭs, feminine noun suffix). Cognates include Latin gula.

parole.significato: beryllium.
parole.testo: From New Latin glucina, from French glucine, from Ancient Greek γλυκύς (glukús, “sweet”) + -um, in reference to the sweet taste of some of its salts.

parole.significato: sweetness
parole.testo: From the New Latin combining form from Ancient Greek γλυκύς (glukús, “sweet”).

parole.significato: Any legume (such as liquorice) of the genus Glycyrrhiza.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek γλυκύρριζα (glukúrrhiza, “sweet root, licorice”). Doublet of licorice.

parole.significato: A member of the genus Glyptodon of extinct giant armadillos.
parole.testo: From the New Latin genus name Glyptodon (from Ancient Greek Ancient Greek γλυπτός (gluptós, “sculptured”) + -odon (“tooth”), 'grooved or carved tooth').

parole.significato: The ramus of the lower jaw of a bird as far as it is naked
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin gnathidium. By surface analysis, gnath- + -idium.

parole.significato: Inflammation of the cheek or upper jaw.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin gnathitis. By surface analysis, gnath- + -itis.

parole.significato: A sex organ that produces gametes; specifically, a testicle or ovary.
parole.testo: From 1880 New Latin gonadēs, plural of New Latin gonas, coined from Ancient Greek γονή (gonḗ, “seed, begetting, birth, offspring”), from γίγνεσθαι (gígnesthai, “be born”).

parole.significato: One of the bluish-green granules that replace the more usual gonidia in certain lichens.
parole.testo: From New Latin gonimium, possibly from Ancient Greek γόνιμος (gónimos, “productive”).

parole.significato: A sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a species of bacteria (the gonococcus) that affects t…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Late Latin gonorrhoea, from Ancient Greek γονόρροια (gonórrhoia), from γόνος (gónos, “sperm, seed, offspring”) + ῥοία (rhoía, “flow”) (ca. 1526). By surface analysis, gono- + -rrhea.

parole.significato: A bacterial disease caused by Klebsiella granulomatis characterized by ulcerative genital lesions, endemic in many less…
parole.testo: A New Latin construction, from grānulōma (“granuloma”) + inguinālis (“inguinal, of the groin”).

parole.significato: To move under the force of gravity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin gravitāt-, past participial stem of gravitō.

parole.significato: The fundamental force of attraction which exists between all matter in the universe that tends to draw bodies towards e…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin gravitātiō. By surface analysis, gravitate + -ion.

parole.significato: Relating to, or resembling, a gooseberry.
parole.testo: From New Latin grossularius, from translingual Grossularia, a subgenus of Ribes, including the gooseberry, from French groseille. The mineral name is in reference to a particular green variety found in Siberia.

parole.significato: Any of a number of species of tree of the genus Guaiacum, native to the West Indies and parts of the Americas.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Spanish guayacán.

parole.significato: a soft, non-cancerous growth, a form of granuloma, resulting from the tertiary stage of syphilis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin gumma, extended in meaning from Late Latin gumma (“gum, resin”), a late form of cummis, cummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi), of Egyptian origin. Doublet of gum (Etymology 2).

parole.significato: Yielding gum or resinous substance, especially said of trees and shrubs in family Guttiferae (now Clusiaceae) that abou…
parole.testo: From guttifer + -ous, from New Latin guttifera (“gum-bearing plant”), from Latin gutta (“drop”).

parole.significato: A small carnivorous mammal, subfamily Galericinae, related to the hedgehogs and resembling a large rat, which inhabits…
parole.testo: From New Latin Gymnura, former genus name, from Ancient Greek γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”).

parole.significato: The pistils/carpels of a flower considered as a group
parole.testo: From New Latin; from gyno- + oecium (from Ancient Greek οἰκῐ́ον (oikĭ́on), diminutive of οἶκος (oîkos, “house”)).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Haloragaceae.
parole.testo: From translingual Haloragaceae + -ous, from New Latin Haloragis + -aceae, formed irregularly from Ancient Greek ἅλς (háls, “salt”) + ῥάξ (rháx, “berry”) (a Pre-Greek / Mediterranean loan).

parole.significato: Any of the flowering plant genus Hamamelis, the witch hazels.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἁμαμηλίς (hamamēlís, “medlar”).

parole.significato: Any of the cichlid fishes of the tribe Haplochromini.
parole.testo: Shortening of New Latin Haplochromis.

parole.significato: Being or relating to a form of arthrodontous peristome:
parole.testo: From New Latin haplolepideus, from Ancient Greek ἁπλόος (haplóos, “two-fold, single”) + λεπίδιον (lepídion, “small plate used to close a tube”).

parole.significato: A pupil of Harrow School, England.
parole.testo: From New Latin Harrovia (“Harrow”) + -an.

parole.significato: A modified arm of any of several male cephalopods that functions as a reproductive organ by transferring sperm to the m…
parole.testo: From New Latin, corresponding to hecto- + Ancient Greek κότυλος (kótulos, “small cup”).

parole.significato: Producing or bearing ivy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin hederifer.

parole.significato: A device that includes a plane mirror which turns so as to keep reflecting sunlight toward a predetermined target, comp…
parole.testo: First use appear c. 1747, from New Latin heliostata, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”) + Latin status (“stationary”). By surface analysis, helio- + -stat.

parole.testo: From New Latin helium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”) (because its presence was first theorised in the Sun's atmosphere) with the suffix + -ium. parole.significato: The inability to see clearly in bright light; day blindness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin hēmeralōpia, from Ancient Greek ἡμεραλωπία (hēmeralōpía). From ἡμέρα (hēmérā, “day”), ἀλαός (alaos, “blind”), and ὄψ (ops, “eye”).

parole.significato: Equus hemionus, the onager or kiang, a kind of wild ass of Tibet.
parole.testo: From New Latin hēmionus, from Ancient Greek ἡμῐ́ονος (hēmĭ́onos, “half ass, mule”).

parole.significato: Total or partial inability to move one side of the body.
parole.testo: From New Latin hemiplegia, from Ancient Greek ἡμιπλήξ (hēmiplḗx), also ἡμιπληγής (hēmiplēgḗs, “stricken on one side”), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “half”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike”). By surface analysis, hemi- + -plegia.

parole.significato: The formation and excretion of sweat.
parole.testo: From New Latin hīdrōsis, from Ancient Greek ῑ̔δρώς (hīdrṓs, “sweat”) + -ωσῐς (-ōsĭs); also synchronically held to end in the suffix -osis.

parole.significato: A warming cathartic medicine made from aloes and canella.
parole.testo: From New Latin hiera picra, from Ancient Greek ἱερᾱ́ πίκρᾱ (hierā́ píkrā, literally “sacred bitterness”).

parole.significato: Eaters of horsemeat.
parole.testo: From the plural of New Latin hippophagus. See hippophagous.

parole.significato: An inferior historian.
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from New Latin historiaster, from Latin historia (“history”) + -aster (suffix denoting incomplete or partial resemblance, and hence sometimes having a derogatory connotation). parole.significato: A human being (Homo sapiens).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin homō sapiēns, from Latin homō (“human being”) + sapiēns (“wise, sensible, judicious”).

parole.significato: The books of the New Testament which were acknowledged as canonical by the early church, as opposed to Antilegomena.
parole.testo: From New Latin homologūmena, from Ancient Greek ὁμολογούμενα (homologoúmena, literally “things agreed upon”), neuter plural form of the present mediopassive participle of ὁμολογέω (homologéō, “to agree with”).

parole.significato: hydrangea (Hydrangea spp.)
parole.testo: From the genus name, New Latin Hortensia, from hortēnsius (“of the garden”), from hortēnsis.

parole.significato: The process of humifying; conversion into humus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin hūmificatiō. By surface analysis, humus + -ification, following humify.

parole.significato: Mercury (chemical element).
parole.testo: From New Latin hydrargyrum (“mercury”). By surface analysis, hydr- + argyr- + -um.

parole.significato: The hollow stem of a hydrozoan
parole.testo: From New Latin hydrocaulus, from hydro- + Ancient Greek καυλός (kaulós, “stalk, stem”).

parole.significato: A flat muscle on either side of the tongue, connecting it with the body and the thyrohyal of the hyoid bone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin hyoglōssus, clipping of musculus hyoglōssus (“hyoglossal muscle”).

parole.significato: A conic section formed by the intersection of a cone with a plane that intersects the base of the cone and is not tange…
parole.testo: From New Latin hyperbola, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολή (huperbolḗ). Doublet of hyperbole.

parole.significato: The condition of having an abnormally high body temperature caused by a failure of the heat-regulating mechanisms of th…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér, “over”) + θέρμη (thérmē, “heat”) + -ία (-ía). By surface analysis, hyper- + -therm + -ia.

parole.significato: An abnormal increase in tightness of muscle tone, common in cerebral palsy.
parole.testo: From New Latin hypertonia, from hyper- + Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos) + -ia. By surface analysis, hyper- + -tonia.

parole.significato: Any of the long, threadlike filaments that form the mycelium of a fungus.
parole.testo: From New Latin hypha, from Ancient Greek ὑφή (huphḗ, “web”).

parole.significato: A formerly defined psychological disorder characterized by excessive preoccupation or worry about having a serious illn…
parole.testo: From New Latin hypochondria (the morbid condition so called, supposed to have its seat in the upper part of the abdomen), from hypochondrium (see English hypochondrium for more).

parole.significato: A mental disorder (in some classifications of such disorders, including ICD-11) characterized by a persistent preoccupa…
parole.testo: From New Latin; by surface analysis, hypochondr(ium) + -iasis. See also hypochondria, hypochondrium, and Wikipedia at hypochondriasis § Etymology.

parole.significato: The upper region of the abdomen, covering the upperribs, at each side of the epigastrium.
parole.testo: From New Latin hypochondrium, from Ancient Greek ὑποχόνδριον (hupokhóndrion, “the soft part of the body below the cartilage and above the navel”), from ὑπό (hupó, “below”) + χόνδρος (khóndros, “cartilage”). See also hypochondria, hypochondriac, and Wikipedia at hypochondriasis § Etymology.

parole.significato: An aftershaft.
parole.testo: From New Latin hypoptilum, from hypo- + Ancient Greek πτίλον (ptílon, “soft feathers, down”).

parole.significato: Abnormally low body temperature; specifically, below 35 degrees Celsius for humans.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ὑπο- (hupo-, “under”) + θέρμη (thérmē, “heat”) + -ία (-ía, “feminine suffix”) . By surface analysis, hypo- + therm- + -ia.

parole.significato: A state of reduced pressure of the intraocular fluid.
parole.testo: From New Latin hypotonia, from hypo- + Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos) + -ia. By surface analysis, hypo- + -tonia.

parole.significato: The petrified remains of hyrax urine and feces produced by the rock hyrax (“Cape hyrax”), Procavia capensis (“P. apensi…
parole.testo: From New Latin hyraceum, from hyrax (stem form hyrac-) + -eus.

parole.significato: Any of several small, paenungulate herbivorous mammals of the family Procaviidae from the order Hyracoidea, with a bulk…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ὕραξ (húrax, “shrewmouse”).

parole.significato: Behavior exhibiting excessive or uncontrollable emotions, in a wide range from joy to panic but usually including anxie…
parole.testo: From New Latin hysteria, a back-formation from Latin hystericus, from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός (husterikós, “suffering in the uterus, hysterical”), from ὑστέρα (hustéra, “womb”). Compare French hystérie.

parole.significato: A plant or fungus that lives on dead or living organic matter.
parole.testo: From New Latin hysterophȳtum, from Ancient Greek ὑστέρα (hustéra, “womb, figuratively the earth”) + φῡτόν (phūtón, “plant”). By surface analysis, hystero- + -phyte.

parole.significato: fish fin.
parole.testo: From New Latin ichthyopterygium, from Ancient Greek ἰχθύς (ikhthús, “fish”) + πτερύγιον (pterúgion, “fin”). By surface analysis, ichthyo- + pterygium.

parole.significato: Any of a group of genetic skin disorders characterized by dry, thickened, scaly skin.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin ichthyōsis. By surface analysis, ichthyo- + -osis. First attested in 1815.

parole.significato: The unconscious impulsive component of the personality in the Freudian psychoanalytic model.
parole.testo: From New Latin id (“it”), chosen by Freud’s translator as a translation of his use of German Es (“it”) as a noun for this concept from the pronoun es (“it”).

parole.significato: A will o' the wisp.
parole.testo: From New Latin ignis fatuus (literally “foolish fire”).

parole.significato: Any of several machines or devices in which a part impacts on another, or on a material.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin impāctor, from impingō + -tor.

parole.significato: In summary; briefly or simply.
parole.testo: Calque of New Latin in nuce, derived from an anecdote in Pliny the Elder, who ascribes to Cicero the claim that the whole Iliad was once written on parchment and enclosed within a nutshell (Naturalis Historia 7.21.85). Compare typologically Czech stručný, stručně (< struk).

parole.significato: In the former or same state.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin in statū quō (literally “in the state in which”). First attested in 1602.

parole.significato: Synonym of in wine, there is truth (one tells the truth under the influence of alcohol)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin in vīnō vēritās (literally “in wine there is truth”), from in (“in”) + vīnō, the ablative singular of vīnum (“wine”) + vēritās (“truth”). parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol In) with an atomic number of 49: a soft silvery-white metal.

parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin īnfectiōsus. By surface analysis, infect + -ious.

parole.significato: Synonym of inferable.
parole.testo: From New Latin īnferibilis.

parole.significato: Any of the many minute aquatic creatures, such as protozoa and unicellular algae, found in freshwater habitats.
parole.testo: From New Latin īnfūsōrium, from Latin īnfundō.

parole.significato: Material introduced into the body by the stomach or alimentary canal.
parole.testo: From New Latin ingerō. See ingest.

parole.significato: Occurring, arising, or functioning without any delay; happening within an imperceptibly brief period of time.
parole.testo: Derived from New Latin īnstāntāneus, from Latin īnstantem. From New Latin īnstāntāneus, from Latin īnstantem.

parole.significato: To soften; tenderize.
parole.testo: From New Latin intenerātus, perfect passive participle of intenerō (from tener (“tender”)), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Of or situated on the inside.
parole.testo: From Middle English internall, internalle, borrowing from New Latin internālis (“of or pertaining to the inner part”), from internus (“inward, internal”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, intern + -al.

parole.significato: A turning inward, particularly
parole.testo: From New Latin intrōversio, from intrōvertere (“to turn within”), from Classical Latin intro (“within”) and vertere (“to turn”). Equivalent to introvert + -sion or intro- + -version.

parole.significato: The part that prolapses into another during an intussusception.
parole.testo: From New Latin, probably from neuter singular of assumed New Latin intussusceptus, the passive past participle of New Latin intussuscipiō (“to take in”). Compare intussuscipiens.

parole.significato: The part that receives the prolapsed part during an intussusception.
parole.testo: From New Latin, probably from present participle of assumed New Latin intussuscipiō (“to take in”). Compare intussusceptum.

parole.significato: To impart vigor, strength, or vitality to.
parole.testo: First attested in 1646; borrowed from New Latin invigōrātus, perfect passive participle of invigōrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, in- + vigor + -ate.

parole.significato: A type of moth, the io moth.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek Ἰώ (Iṓ, “Io”).

parole.significato: Inflected to indicate that an act or state of being is not a fact.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin irreālis (“intangible, immaterial”), from Latin in- (“un-: not”) + reālis (“real, material, composed of physical things”), from res (“thing”) + -ālis (“-al: forming adjectives”). Doublet of irreal.

parole.significato: Local disturbance in blood circulation due to mechanical obstruction of the blood supply (for example, embolism, thromb…
parole.testo: From New Latin ischaemia, from Ancient Greek ἴσχαιμος (ískhaimos, “stoppage of blood flow”), from ῐ̓́σχω (ĭ́skhō, “to hold back, restrain; to stay, stop”) + αἷμᾰ (haîmă, “blood”). The plural form ischemiae is also from New Latin ischaemiae.

parole.significato: pain in the region of the ischium; sciatica
parole.testo: From New Latin ischialgia, from Latin ischion + -algia.

parole.significato: A function between metric spaces (or on a single metric space) having the property that the distance between two images…

parole.significato: Relating to or caused by hard ticks.
parole.testo: From New Latin Ixodes (from Ancient Greek ἰξώδης (ixṓdēs)) + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Japonic language family.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin japonicus.

parole.significato: A species of camellia (Camellia japonica), a native flower of Japan, bearing beautiful red or white flowers.
parole.testo: From New Latin iaponicus (“Japanese”), from Iaponia.

parole.significato: Any of several plants originally native to Japan.
parole.testo: From New Latin japō̆nica, the species name.

parole.significato: A member of the Society of Jesus.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin Iēsūīta, from Latin Iēsūs + -īta.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Jesuits, or to their principles and methods.
parole.testo: From New Latin Iēsūīticus, from Iēsūīta + Latin -icus. By surface analysis, Jesuit + -ic.

parole.significato: Synonym of microspecies
parole.testo: New Latin, from Alexis Jordan †1897 French biologist + -on, on analogy with taxon.

parole.significato: The neck or throat.
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin jugulum (“the collarbone; the hollow part of the neck above the collarbone; the throat”), diminutive of jugum (“a yoke, collar”).

parole.significato: A device to compress the penis, used to prevent masturbation in Victorian times.
parole.testo: From New Latin iugum pēnis (“yoke/collar of the penis”), pēnis being a genitive.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, occurring in, or typifying any one or more of the editions of texts published by the Giunti family o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Juntīnus.

parole.significato: Containing potassium.
parole.testo: From New Latin kalium + -ian.

parole.significato: potassium.
parole.testo: From New Latin kalium.

parole.significato: movement
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek κῑνέω (kīnéō, “to move”).

parole.significato: Any of the twining leguminous plants related to the bean, especially the hyacinth bean.
parole.testo: From the taxonomic New Latin Lablab.

parole.significato: Giardia lamblia, an intestinal parasite that causes giardiasis.
parole.testo: From New Latin, Lambl + -ia, named after Austrian physician Vilém Dušan Lambl (1824–1895).

parole.significato: To assemble from thin sheets glued together to make a thicker sheet.
parole.testo: First attested in 1666; borrowed from New Latin laminātus, perfect passive participle of laminō (attested since the first quarter of the 16th century), from Latin lāmina (“thin sheet of metal/other material”), see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3).

parole.significato: laryngospasm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin laryngismus, from the Ancient Greek λαρυγγισμός (larungismós, “a croaking”), from λάρυγξ (lárunx), whence also larynx. By surface analysis, laryng- + -ismus.

parole.significato: An inflammation of the larynx, typically resulting in hoarseness.
parole.testo: Attested since 1822 C.E. Learned borrowing from New Latin laryngitis, from larynx + -itis. By surface analysis, laryng- + -itis.

parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin larynx, from Ancient Greek λᾰ́ρῠγξ (lắrŭnx, “larynx; windpipe; gullet, throat”).

parole.significato: Any of several tinctures of opium, once widely used for various medical purposes and as a recreational drug.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from lādanum (“a gum resin”), from Ancient Greek λᾱ́δανον (lā́danon). Originally the same word as ladanum, labdanum, compare French laudanum, Italian laudano, ladano. parole.significato: The Viburnum tinus, an evergreen shrub or tree of the south of Europe, which flowers during the winter months.
parole.testo: From New Latin laurustinus, Latin laurus (“laurel”) + tīnus (“Viburnum tinus”). See laurel.

parole.significato: Either of two babblers of the genus Leiothrix within the family Leiothrichidae.
parole.testo: From New Latin leio- (“smooth”) + Ancient Greek θρίξ (thríx, “hair”).

parole.significato: A closed curve having the shape of a figure eight or an infinity symbol (∞).
parole.testo: First attested in 1781; borrowed from New Latin lēmniscāta (figūra), substantivized from lēmniscātus (“decorated with ribbons”), from lēmniscus (“a sort of ribbon”).

parole.significato: One of the small, oval, rounded spots upon the stem or branch of a plant, from which the underlying tissues may protrud…
parole.testo: From New Latin lenticella, diminutive of Latin lēns (“lentil”); compare French lenticelle.

parole.significato: Synonym of lenticel.
parole.testo: From New Latin lenticella, from Latin lenticula + -ella.

parole.significato: Covered with scurfy scales.

parole.significato: The study of leprosy, particularly (medicine) its diagnosis and treatment.
parole.testo: From New Latin leprologia, from Medieval Latin leprōsia (“leprosy”) + -logia (“-logy”), from leprōsus (“leprous”) + -ia, from lepra (“leprosy”) + -ōsus (“-ose”), q.v. Equivalent to leprosy + -ology.

parole.significato: An area of inflammation in the skin symptomatic of leprosy
parole.testo: From New Latin leproma, equivalent to lepra (“leprosy”) + -oma (“mass or tumor related to”).

parole.significato: diethyl ether, used as an anaesthetic agent.
parole.testo: From New Latin lēthēon, from Ancient Greek λήθη (lḗthē, “forgetting, forgetfulness”).

parole.significato: One who, or something which, lifts something else, as:
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin levātor (“one that lifts or raises”). Doublet of lever.

parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin levātor labiī superiōris ālaeque nāsī (“lifter of the upper lip and of the wing of the nose”).

parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin levātor palpebrae superiōris (“lifter of the superior eyelid”).

parole.significato: A portion of the pubococcygeus muscle that helps to support the prostate gland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin levātor prostatae (“lifter of the prostate”).

parole.significato: A muscle arising from the temporal bone and the cartilage of the Eustachian tube and descending to insert into the midl…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin levātor vēlī palātīnī (“lifter of the palatine veil”).

parole.significato: To cause to rise in the air and float, as if in defiance of gravity.
parole.testo: First attested in 1673; borrowed from New Latin levitātus, perfect passive participle of levitō (“to levitate; to have one's motion directed upward, as opposed to the downward motion induced by gravity”) (first attested c. 1670), modeled on gravitō (“to gravitate”) (← Latin gravis (“heavy”)), from l

parole.significato: The fragrant wood of several shrubs and trees, especially of species Convolvulus scoparius and Convolvulus floridus (Co…
parole.testo: From New Latin lignum rhodium (literally “rosy wood”), from Ancient Greek ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”).

parole.significato: A longitudinal band of muscular fibres, situated on the undersurface of the tongue, lying in the interval between the h…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin linguālis, ellipsis of mūsculus linguālis (“lingual muscle”). Doublet of lingual.

parole.significato: The simplest alkali metal, the lightest solid element, and the third lightest chemical element (symbol Li) with an atom…
parole.testo: From New Latin lithium, from Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “stone”) + -ium.

parole.significato: Synonym of kaolinite.
parole.testo: From New Latin lithomarga, from Ancient Greek λιθος (lithos, “stone”) + Latin marga (“marl”). Equivalent to litho- + marge.

parole.significato: An authoritative passage from a standard work that is often quoted as an illustration; a classic case or example.
parole.testo: From New Latin locus classicus (literally “classical place”).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Logania of plants native to Australia and New Zealand.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Logania (“the genus name”), after the botanist James Logan.

parole.significato: A long muscle in the body.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin longus (“long”), clipping of musculus longus (“long muscle”).

parole.significato: A muscle of either side of the front and upper portion of the neck that arises from the third to sixth cervical vertebr…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin longus capitis, clipping of musculus longus capitis (“long muscle of the head”).

parole.significato: The central keel-bearing part of the sternum in birds, or the keel itself.
parole.testo: From New Latin lophosteon, from Ancient Greek λόφος (lóphos, “crest”) + ὀστέον (ostéon, “bone”).

parole.significato: Having the form of a thong or strap.

parole.significato: Worm-like.

parole.significato: Synonym of lumbrical.
parole.testo: From New Latin lumbricalis, from lumbricus (“intestinal worm, earthworm”).

parole.significato: A resinous extract of Lycopus virginicus, formerly used as an internal hemostatic.
parole.testo: From New Latin Lycopersicon.

parole.significato: Synonym of lymph node.
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin lymphoglandula, from lympha (“clear water”) + glandula (“a small acorn”), equivalent to lympho- + glandula.

parole.significato: Synonym of lymph node.
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin lymphonōdus, from lympha (“clear water”) + nōdus (“a knot, knob, node”); equivalent to lympho- + nodus.

parole.significato: Shaped like a lyre.
parole.testo: From New Latin lyrātus, from lyra (“lyre”). By surface analysis, lyre + -ate.

parole.significato: Jumbled, mixed.

parole.significato: A large chaeta found in certain organisms
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin macrochaeta, equivalent to macro- + chaeta.

parole.significato: The chemical element with an atomic number of 12. It is a light, easily flammable, silvery-white alkaline earth metal.
parole.testo: From New Latin magnēsium, from Ancient Greek μαγνησία (magnēsía), after Μαγνησία (Magnēsía, “Magnesia”), a region in Thessaly. Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy, as a modification of his original suggestion, magnium.

parole.significato: mantis (insect)
parole.testo: From New Latin Mantidae.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or resembling the order Mantodea.
parole.testo: From New Latin Mantoidea.

parole.significato: Notes in the margin of a document.
parole.testo: From New Latin marginālia (cf. margināle (neuter singular (adjective / noun)), from Medieval Latin neuter plural of marginālis (“on the periphery”), from Latin margō (“border, edge”). By surface analysis, marginal + -ia. Compare margin.

parole.significato: A representation of a sea view.
parole.testo: From New Latin marinorama, from Latin marīnus (“marine”) + -orama.

parole.significato: Being the process of the temporal bone behind the ear.

parole.significato: masturbate

parole.significato: A consonant letter used to represent a vowel sound in Semitic scripts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin māter lēctiōnis (literally “mother of reading”), calque of Medieval Hebrew אֵם קְרִיאָה (ʾēm qərîʾā).

parole.significato: A small, antenna-like sensory appendage in certain invertebrates emerging from the maxilla.
parole.testo: Calque of New Latin palpus maxillaris.

parole.significato: Any mechanical means for the conversion or control of motion, or the transmission or control of power.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin mechanismus.

parole.significato: The region in mammals between the pleural sacs, containing the heart and all of the thoracic viscera except the lungs.
parole.testo: From New Latin mediastīnum, from Medieval Latin mediastīnus (“middling; middle”), from Latin mediastīnus (“a common servant”).

parole.significato: The middle finger.

parole.significato: The lower portion of the brain stem.
parole.testo: From New Latin medulla (“inner part, marrow, pith”) and New Latin oblongata (“elongated, oblong”).

parole.significato: Any of a group of naturally occurring dark pigments, especially the pigment found in skin, hair, fur, and feathers.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek stem of μέλας (mélas, “black”) + -in; by surface analysis, melan(o)- + -in.

parole.significato: The passage of dark, tarry stools containing blood, a result of upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
parole.testo: From New Latin melaena, based on Ancient Greek μέλαινα (mélaina, “black”).

parole.significato: Any of a number of birds in the genus Melidectes in the honeyeater family, endemic to New Guinea and New Britain.
parole.testo: From New Latin Melidectes, from Ancient Greek μέλι (méli, “honey”) + δέκτης (déktēs, “receiver”).

parole.significato: The annual fixed liturgical cycle of services used in the Eastern Orthodox and Greek-Catholic Churches, containing a li…
parole.testo: From New Latin mēnaion, from Ancient Greek μηναῖος (mēnaîos, “lunar”).

parole.significato: A membrane, especially one of the three membranes lining the skull and vertebral canal and enclosing the brain and spin…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin mēninx, from Ancient Greek μῆνῐγξ (mênĭnx, “membrane of the eye; membrane enclosing the brain; eardrum”).

parole.significato: An internode.

parole.significato: A worker ant that is deformed by parasitic nematodes.
parole.testo: From New Latin mermithergata, from Ancient Greek μέρμις (mérmis, “cord, string”) + ἐργάτης (ergátēs, “worker”).

parole.significato: The mesogastrium.
parole.testo: From New Latin mesogastrium, from Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos, “middle”) + γαστήρ (gastḗr, “belly”).

parole.significato: The dorsal portion of the mesothorax of insects.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek, meaning "middle of the back".

parole.significato: The middle portion of the foot in the gastropods and pteropods.
parole.testo: From New Latin mesopodium, from meso- + -podium.

parole.significato: The fold of peritoneum that attaches the testis to the dorsal wall of the body cavity or scrotum.

parole.significato: The dorsal portion of the metathorax of insects
parole.testo: From New Latin metanōtum, from Ancient Greek μετα- (meta-) + νῶτον (nôton).

parole.significato: The posterior division of the foot in the Gastropoda and Pteropoda.
parole.testo: From New Latin metapodium, from Ancient Greek μετα- (meta-) + πούς (poús). By surface analysis, meta- + -pode.

parole.significato: The posterolateral ossification in the sternum of birds, or the part resulting from such ossification.
parole.testo: From New Latin metosteon, from Ancient Greek μετα- (meta-, “after”) + ὀστέον (ostéon, “bone”).

parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin mīcella, from mīca (“crumb”) + -ella.

parole.significato: A member of the superseded taxonomic order Micropoda, which possess a diminutive foot or lack one, such as oysters.
parole.testo: From New Latin Micropoda, from micro- + -poda.

parole.significato: The branch of petrology that studies minerals.

parole.significato: molybdenum poisoning

parole.significato: A book describing or giving an account of monasteries.

parole.significato: A germ in that stage of development in which its form is simply a non-nucleated mass of protoplasm.

parole.significato: The doctrine of the oneness and unity of reality, despite the appearance of diversity in the world.

parole.significato: A type of cyme on which each single axis bears one flower.

parole.significato: A canoe or boat made from a hollowed out tree.

parole.significato: Any tree of the genus Mora of large South American trees.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to mucilage; of, pertaining to, or resembling mucus; slimy and viscous.

parole.significato: mucus.

parole.significato: The hardy rose Rosa multiflora

parole.significato: The vegetative part of any fungus, consisting of a mass of branching, threadlike hyphae, often underground.

parole.significato: megakaryocyte or osteoclast

parole.significato: Relating to or in the region of the lower jaw and the hyoid apparatus, or the mylohyoid muscle.

parole.significato: The mylohyoid muscle.

parole.significato: The muscular substance of the heart; the middle of the three layers forming the outer wall of the human heart.

parole.testo: From New Latin pharynx, from Ancient Greek φάρυγξ (phárunx, “throat”), akin to modern Greek φάρυγγας (fáryngas, “pharynx”).

parole.significato: The part of the alimentary canal and respiratory tract that extends from the back of the mouth and nasal cavity to the…
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin pharynx, from Ancient Greek φᾰ́ρῠγξ (phắrŭnx, “throat”).

parole.significato: A distinguishable part of a sequence or cycle occurring over time.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin phasis, borrowed from Ancient Greek φάσις (phásis, “appearance”), from φᾰ(ν)- (phă(n)-, root of φαίνω (phaínō, “to bring to light; to appear”)) + -σῐς (-sĭs). Compare phantasm and see face.

parole.significato: Any of several climbing plants, of the genus Philodendron, native to America and the West Indies that are often grown a…
parole.testo: From New Latin philodendron, from Ancient Greek φῐλόδενδρον (phĭlódendron), neuter of φῐλόδενδρος (phĭlódendros, “loving trees”). First known use: 1877.

parole.significato: An inflammation, especially of the internal organs.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek φλεγμᾰσία (phlegmăsía, “inflammation”), from φλέγμα (phlégma, “flame”) (whence also phlegm).

parole.significato: The hypothetical fiery principle formerly assumed to be a necessary constituent of combustible bodies and to be given u…
parole.testo: From New Latin phlogiston, coined by Georg Ernst Stahl in 1702, from Ancient Greek φλογιστόν (phlogistón), neuter of φλογιστός (phlogistós, “burnt up, inflammable”), from φλογίζω (phlogízō, “to set fire to”), from φλόξ (phlóx, “flame”).

parole.significato: Any flowering plant of the genus Phlox.
parole.testo: From New Latin Phlox, from Ancient Greek φλόξ (phlóx, “flame”).

parole.significato: An irrational, abnormal, or obsessive fear (of something).
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1790, from words ending in -phobia, ultimately from Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”). Compare ism, from -ism, itis, from -itis, and ana, from -ana.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the diaphragm
parole.testo: From New Latin phrenicus, from Ancient Greek φρήν (phrḗn, “diaphragm”).

parole.significato: A local division of the people; a clan or tribe.
parole.testo: From New Latin phȳlē, from Ancient Greek φῡλή (phūlḗ, “a union of individuals into a community”).

parole.significato: phyllode
parole.testo: From New Latin phyllōdium, from Ancient Greek φυλλώδης (phullṓdēs, “leaflike”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Physalis.
parole.testo: From New Latin Physalis, coined by Linnaeus from Ancient Greek φυσαλλίς (phusallís, “bladder, wind instrument”), from φυσιόω (phusióō, “to puff up, blow up”), φυσώ (phusṓ).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Phytolacca of herbaceous plants; the poke or pokeweed.
parole.testo: From New Latin phytolacca, from Ancient Greek φῠτόν (phŭtón, “plant”) + Italian lacca (“crimson lake”).

parole.significato: A plant-like animal; a zoophyte.
parole.testo: From phyto- + zoon, from New Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: The uppermost layer of hyphae in the pileus of a fungal fruit body.
parole.testo: From New Latin pileus + pellis.

parole.significato: Having lobes with incisions that extend almost, or up to midrib.
parole.testo: From New Latin pinnatisectus, from Latin pinnātus (“feathered”) + sectum, past participle of secō (“to cut”).

parole.significato: A form of endocytosis in which material enters a cell through its membrane and is incorporated in vesicles for digestio…
parole.testo: From New Latin pīnocytōsis, from Ancient Greek πῑ́νω (pī́nō, “to drink”) + cyt- + -osis.

parole.significato: A gluteal muscle which arises from the front of the sacrum and the ischium or sacrotuberous ligament, passes out of the…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin pirifōrmis, ellipsis of mūsculus pirifōrmis (“pear-shaped muscle”). Doublet of piriform.

parole.significato: An archegonium.
parole.testo: From New Latin pistillidium, from Latin pistillum (“pestle”) + -idium.

parole.significato: Any of several varieties of skin diseases characterized by the shedding of flakes or scales, such as dandruff.
parole.testo: From New Latin pityriasis, from Koine Greek πιτυρίασις (pituríasis), from Ancient Greek πίτῡρον (pítūron, “bran”).

parole.significato: An organ in most mammals during gestation that supplies food and oxygen to the foetus and passes back waste. It is on t…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin placenta (literally “flat cake”), an ellipsis of phrases such as placenta uterī (literally “womb cake”) and placenta uterīna (literally “uterine cake”), because of the flat round shape of the afterbirth. Doublet of palacsinta and palatschinke.

parole.significato: A display museum in which images of stars and other astronomical phenomena are projected onto a domed ceiling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin planētārium. Equivalent to planet + -arium.

parole.significato: A procedure in which whole blood is removed from a donor or patient and centrifuged to isolate blood cells that are res…
parole.testo: From New Latin plasma + Ancient Greek ἀφαίρεσις (aphaíresis, “removal”).

parole.significato: A semiaquatic monotreme from eastern Australia with a bill resembling that of a duck, that has a mole-like body, a tail…
parole.testo: From New Latin Platypus (originally a genus name already in use for a type of beetle), from Ancient Greek πλατύπους (platúpous, “flat-footed”), from πλατύς (platús, “flat”) + πούς (poús, “foot”). Piecewise doublet of flatfoot.

parole.significato: A superficial muscle of the human neck that overlaps the sternocleidomastoid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin platysma, from Ancient Greek πλᾰ́τῠσμᾰ (plắtŭsmă, “flat object”), from πλᾰτῠ́νω (plătŭ́nō, “widen”) + -μᾰ (-mă, “nominal suffix”).

parole.significato: The quality of deserving applause, praiseworthiness; something worthy of praise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin plausibilitās.

parole.significato: The use of the first-person plural instead of the first-person singular with the intent of referring to oneself more mo…
parole.testo: Calque of New Latin plūrālis modestiae.

parole.significato: Spanning several years in duration or interval.
parole.testo: From New Latin plūrennis + English -ial, after -ennial (compare pluriennial).

parole.significato: Lasting a few years
parole.testo: From New Latin plūriennis + English -ial, after -ennial (compare plurennial).

parole.significato: The study of the respiratory system and organs.
parole.testo: From New Latin pneumologia, from Ancient Greek πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”) + -logia (“-logy”). By surface analysis, pneumo- + -logy.

parole.significato: A nocturnal monster in Ancient Greece that would choke its victims; incubus; nightmare.
parole.testo: From New Latin pnīgalion, from Ancient Greek πνῑγαλίων (pnīgalíōn, “nightmare”), from πνῑ́γω (pnī́gō, “to throttle, strangle”).

parole.significato: A stalk which bears the fructification in some lichens, such as the reindeer moss.
parole.testo: From New Latin podetium, from Ancient Greek πούς (poús, “foot”).

parole.significato: An unskilled poet.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin poētaster. By surface analysis, poet + -aster.

parole.significato: Producing pollen
parole.testo: From pollen + -i- + -ferous, or directly from New Latin pollinifer, polliniferus.

parole.significato: A rare, highly radioactive chemical element (symbol Po) with atomic number 84.
parole.testo: From New Latin polonium, from Medieval Latin Polonia (“Poland”), named after Marie Curie's homeland.

parole.significato: Having many glands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin polyadenus.

parole.significato: A solid figure with many flat faces and straight edges.
parole.testo: From New Latin polyedron, from Ancient Greek πολύεδρος (polúedros, “having many seats”), from πολυ- (polu-, “many”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”); compare French polyèdre. By surface analysis, poly- + -hedron.

parole.significato: Having, or assuming, a variety of forms, characters, or styles
parole.testo: From New Latin polymorphus, from Ancient Greek πολύμορφος (polúmorphos, “multiform, manifold”), from πολυ- (polu-, “many, much”) + μορφή (morphḗ, “form, shape”). By surface analysis, poly- + -morphous.

parole.significato: A polyzoary
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin polyzoārium, from polyzoa + -arium.

parole.significato: A colony of polyzoa.
parole.testo: From New Latin polyzoārium (“polyzoary”), from New Latin polyzoa + -ary.

parole.significato: A pine tree of very large size, native to western North America (Pinus ponderosa).
parole.testo: From the specific epithet, New Latin ponderōsa (“heavy”), in reference to the wood.

parole.significato: A method for finding the middle term of a syllogism in Aristotlean analytics.
parole.testo: From New Latin pons asinorum, from Latin pōns (“bridge”) + genitive plural of asinus (“donkey”). Literally, “bridge of donkeys”.

parole.significato: An addendum to a letter, added after the author's signature.
parole.testo: From New Latin postscriptum, from Latin, neuter of postscriptus, past participle of postscrībō (“write after”), from post (“after”) + scrībō (“write”). By surface analysis, post- + script.

parole.significato: A product resulting from a process, event, or course of action.
parole.testo: From New Latin praecipitātum. Equivalent to Latin praecipitō + -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: In preparation for the main matter; initial, introductory, preparatory.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin praelīmināris, formed from prae- (“before”) + līmen (“threshold”) + -āris (adjectival suffix); compare Latin līmināris (“of or belonging to a threshold”). Compare French préliminaire.

parole.significato: Situated above the kidneys, or at the junction of the vena cava and the renal vein.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin praerēnālis and equal to pre- + renal.

parole.significato: Inability of the eye, due to ageing, to focus on nearby objects.
parole.testo: From New Latin presbyōpia, from Ancient Greek πρέσβυς (présbus, “old man”), and New Latin -ōpia (“vision problem”), from Ancient Greek ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”). By surface analysis, presby- + -opia.

parole.significato: A waterspout.
parole.testo: From New Latin prēstēr, from Ancient Greek πρηστήρ (prēstḗr, “hurricane or waterspout attended with lightning; (in plural) veins of the neck when swollen by anger”).

parole.significato: Preventing, hindering, or acting as an obstacle to.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin praeventīvus. Equivalent to prevent + -ive.

parole.significato: Pregnant or giving birth for the first time.
parole.testo: From New Latin prīmiparus, from prīmus (“first”) + pariō (“to give birth”).

parole.significato: The addition of a leap day to the lunar calendar.
parole.testo: From New Latin proemptōsis, from Ancient Greek προ- (pro-, “before”) + ἔμπτωσις (émptōsis, “falling”).

parole.significato: Being the product of two consecutive integers.
parole.testo: Apparently from New Latin pronicus, a misspelling of Latin promicus, from Ancient Greek προμήκης (promḗkēs, “elongated, oblong”), but the spelling has been pronic from its earliest known occurrence in English (Leonhard Euler, Opera Omnia, series 1, volume 15).

parole.significato: Agitation, publicity, public communication aimed at influencing an audience and furthering an agenda.
parole.testo: From New Latin prōpāganda, short for Congregātiō dē Prōpāgandā Fidē (“a committee of cardinals established in 1622 by Gregory XV to supervise foreign missions”, literally “congregation for propagating the faith”), and properly the ablative feminine gerundive of Latin prōpāgō (“propagate”). parole.significato: An inclination, disposition, tendency, preference, or attraction.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin prōpensitās. By surface analysis, propense (“inclined, disposed”) + -ity.

parole.significato: An early larval form of a trematode worm; a redia.
parole.testo: From New Latin proscōlēx, from Ancient Greek προ- (pro-) + σκώληξ (skṓlēx).

parole.significato: Artificial, acting as a substitute for part of the body; relating to prosthesis.
parole.testo: From New Latin prostheticus, from Ancient Greek προσθετικός (prosthetikós, “adding; repletive; giving additional power”), from πρόσθεσις (prósthesis, “addition”), from προστίθημι (prostíthēmi, “I add”), from πρός (prós, “towards”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “I place”). By surface analysis, prosth- + -etic.

parole.significato: The part of the avian stomach, between the crop and the gizzard, that secretes digestive enzymes.
parole.testo: From New Latin proventriculus (19th century), from pro- + ventriculus.

parole.significato: Divination by drawing pebbles from a pile.
parole.testo: From New Latin psēphomantia, from Ancient Greek ψῆφος (psêphos, “pebble used for casting a vote”), + -mancy.

parole.significato: False history.
parole.testo: From pseudo- + history, coined around 1815, after New Latin pseudo-historia (since 1654 or earlier according to OED).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to or lying in the region of the inferior part of the sphenoid bone of the vertebrate skull.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin pterygoīdēs, from Ancient Greek πτερῠγοειδής (pterŭgoeidḗs, “like a wing”), from πτέρῠξ (ptérŭx, “a wing”) + -ο- (-o-) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-like, -oid”).

parole.significato: A bladder-like pouch on the head of schizophoran flies that by expanding enables the fly to emerge from its puparium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ptilīnum, itself an adaptation of the French ptiline.

parole.significato: The appearance or study of feathers on a bird, including factors such as their texture or shape.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ptilōsis, from the Ancient Greek πτῐ́λωσῐς (ptĭ́lōsĭs).

parole.significato: The way in which an individual leaf is folded in the bud.
parole.testo: From New Latin ptyxis, from Ancient Greek πτύξις (ptúxis, “a folding”).

parole.significato: Part of the levator ani muscle that loops around the vagina in women.
parole.testo: From pubo- + New Latin vaginalis.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or associated with the puerperium (the first month of postpartum), or, sometimes also
parole.testo: From New Latin puerperālis, from Latin puerpera (“woman in childbirth”), from puer (“child”) + pariō (“to bear”).

parole.significato: Dagger-shaped.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin pugioniformis, from Latin pūgiō (“dagger”). By surface analysis, Latin pugion + -i- + form.

parole.significato: Having lungs or similar organs.
parole.testo: From New Latin pulmōnātus (“having lungs”), from pulmō (“lung”) + -ātus.

parole.significato: To expand and contract rhythmically; to throb or to beat, exhibit a pulse.
parole.testo: Perhaps formed within English as a back-formation from pulsation (attested from the early 15th century, in Middle English). A figurative derivation from New Latin pulsō, pulsātum (“(of an organ) to pulse, to emit a pulse”, intransitive) is also possible, itself a back-formation of New Latin pulsātiō

parole.significato: An insect in the development stage between larva and adult.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin, from a special use of Latin pūpa (“little girl; doll, puppet”). Doublet of pupe; compare also puppet, puppy.

parole.significato: An enclosing case of a pupa that is formed from the exoskeleton of an insect's final stage before pupation.
parole.testo: A New Latin coinage from pūpa (“pupa”, originally “little girl; doll”) + -ārium (“place”), equivalent to English pupa + -arium.

parole.significato: In certain fungi, a flask-shaped cavity from the surface of the inner walls of which spores are produced.
parole.testo: From New Latin pycnidium, from pycno- (“dense”) + -idium.

parole.significato: The caudal plate of trilobites, crustacea, and certain insects.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin pygidium, By surface analysis, pygo- + -idium.

parole.significato: The passage between the iter and optocoele in the brain.
parole.testo: From New Latin pyla, from Ancient Greek πύλη (púlē, “gate, entrance”).

parole.significato: pus
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek πύον (púon, “pus”), from Proto-Indo-European *puH-; compare Sanskrit पूयति (pūyati, “stinks, rots”), Ancient Greek πύθω (púthō, “to rot”), Gothic 𐍆𐌿𐌻𐍃 (fuls, “foul”), Old English ful (“foul”).

parole.significato: The small pyramid which crowns or completes an obelisk or pyramid.
parole.testo: From New Latin pyramidion, from Latin pyramis. See pyramid.

parole.significato: A nutlet resembling a seed, or the stone of a drupe, comprising the endocarp and the kernel.
parole.testo: From New Latin pyrēna, from Ancient Greek πῡρήν (pūrḗn, “fruit-stone”).

parole.significato: Caused by, pertaining to or resulting in fever.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin pyreticus, from Ancient Greek πυρετικός (puretikós, “febrile”), from πυρετός (puretós, “fever”), from πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).

parole.significato: Pear-shaped.
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin pyrifōrmis, from pyrum (“a pear”) + -fōrmis (“-form, -shaped”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of pyriformis.

parole.significato: A yellowish organic keto acid, 2-oxopropanoic acid, which occurs as an intermediate in many metabolic processes, especi…
parole.testo: From New Latin acidum pyruvicum, from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) + ūva (“grape”) + -icum (neuter singular of -icus), from its being produced by the dry distillation of racemic acid, originally derived from grapes. By surface analysis, pyr(e) + Latin uv(a) + -ic.

parole.significato: A seed capsule in the form of a box, the seeds being released when the top splits off.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek πυξίδιον (puxídion), diminutive of πῠξῐ́ς (pŭxĭ́s, “box”).

parole.significato: A grammatical number referring to four (or more) things.
parole.testo: From New Latin quadrālis, from quadru- (“four-”) + -ālis.

parole.significato: A polygon with four sides.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin quadrilaterus + -al.

parole.significato: A period of five hundred years, half a millennium.
parole.testo: From New Latin quincentennium (“500-year period”). Compare the classical Latin form quingenti (“500”). Equivalent to quin- (“five”) + centennium (“century, 100-year period”). Cognate with quincentenary and quincentennial.

parole.significato: Synonym of cinchona in all its senses.
parole.testo: From New Latin quinquina, variant of cinchona.

parole.significato: The spinal column, or the vertebrae of the spine.
parole.testo: From New Latin rhachis/rachis, from Ancient Greek ῥάχις (rhákhis, “spine, ridge”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to, or affected by, rickets (“a disorder of infancy and early childhood due to a deficiency of vitamin…
parole.testo: From rachitis (“rickets”) + -ic (suffix forming adjectives from nouns with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’), possibly modelled after French rachitique or Late Latin rachiticus. parole.significato: Rickets.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin rachitis, used by the British physician Francis Glisson (1597–1677) to refer to rickets, from Koine Greek ῥαχῖτις (rhakhîtis) (in ῥαχῖτις νόσος (rhakhîtis nósos, “spinal inflammation”, literally “spinal disease”)), the feminine form of ῥαχίτης (rhakhítēs, “in or of

parole.significato: A small branch of a root; a rootlet.
parole.testo: From New Latin rādīcella, from radic- (“root”) + -ella. Doublet of radicle and radicula. By surface analysis, Latin radic- + -el (“diminutive”).

parole.significato: Shaped like a frog; resembling a frog.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin rānifōrmis.

parole.significato: A frog-eater; a creature that eats frogs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin rānivorus.

parole.significato: frog-eating
parole.testo: From New Latin rānivorus.

parole.significato: A seamlike ridge or furrow on an organ, bodily tissue, or other structure, typically marking the line where two halves…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin raphē, from Ancient Greek ῥᾰφή (rhăphḗ, “seam; suture”).

parole.significato: Synonym of rectorship.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin rēctōrātus.

parole.significato: The terminal part of the large intestine through which feces pass after exiting the colon, but before leaving the body…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin rectum, clipping of Latin rectum intestinum (literally “the straight intestine”), rectum, neuter of rectus (“straight”). See right.

parole.significato: A paired muscle running vertically on each side of the anterior wall of the abdomen in humans and some other mammals.
parole.testo: From New Latin rectus abdominis, from Latin rēctus + abdōminis.

parole.significato: Drawing upon, invoking, or referring back to itself.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin recursīvus. Equivalent to recurse + -ive.

parole.significato: The act of loving in return.
parole.testo: From the New Latin redamantia, from the Classical Latin redamō (“to requite love”, transitive verb).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an ecclesiastical region.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin regionarius, referring to a deacon in charge of one of the seven wards of Rome, from Latin regiō + -ārius. Equivalent to region + -ary. Doublet of regionarius.

parole.significato: Crawling, creeping.
parole.testo: From reptatory (“crawling, creeping”) + -al (suffix forming adjectives). parole.significato: Relating to respiration or the organs of respiration; breathing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin respīrātōrius, equal to respire + -atory.

parole.significato: Having the structure of a net or a network; netlike.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin rēticulāris, from Latin rēticulum (“little net”).

parole.significato: Part of the eye of an invertebrate which corresponds in function with the retina of a vertebrate, hypothetical membrane…
parole.testo: From New Latin retineum, from Medieval Latin retina. By surface analysis, retin(a) + -eum.

parole.significato: One of the group of pigmented cells that surround the retinophorae of invertebrates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin rētinula, diminutive of Medieval Latin rētina. By surface analysis, retin(a) + -ula.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or employing reverberation or deflection.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin reverberatorius; by surface analysis, reverberate + -ory.

parole.significato: A simple, straight spicule.
parole.testo: From a New Latin form of Ancient Greek ῥάβδος (rhábdos, “rod”).

parole.significato: A type of chronic nasal inflammation where there is little to no nasal secretion, causing discomfort in breathing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin rhinitis sicca (“dry rhinitis”).

parole.significato: Compulsive nose-picking; the insertion of a finger into one's nose.
parole.testo: From rhino- (“nose, nasal”) + Latin tillexis (“habit of plucking”, see below) + -o- + -mania (“obsession”). parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Rhipsalis, epiphytic flowering plants in the cactus family, often known as mistletoe cacti.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ῥίψ (rhíps, “wickerwork”) + Latin -alis (“-al”).

parole.significato: A rare, hard, silvery-white, inert metallic chemical element (symbol Rh) with an atomic number of 45.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin rhodium, from Ancient Greek ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”), because of the colour of its salts' solutions.

parole.significato: An Archimedean solid with 62 regular faces (20 triangles, 30 squares, and 12 pentagons), 60 vertices and 120 edges.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin rhombicosidodecaēdron (coined by the German astronomer and mathematician Johannes Kepler (1571–1630) in his work Harmonices Mundi Libri V (The Harmony of the World in Five Books, 1619)), a blend of Latin rhomb(us) + īcos(aedron) + -i- + dodecaēdron. parole.significato: One of the small sensory tentacular structures of various jellyfish species.
parole.testo: From New Latin rhopalium, from Ancient Greek ῥοπαλιον (rhopalion), diminutive of ῥόπαλον (rhópalon, “club”).

parole.significato: Having a series of fleshy lobes or filaments.

parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin urtīcāria, from Latin urtīca (“nettle”) + -āria.

parole.significato: A world in which everything and everyone works in perfect harmony.
parole.testo: From New Latin Ūtopia, the name of a fictional island possessing a seemingly perfect socio-politico-legal system in the book Utopia (1516) by Sir Thomas More. Coined from Ancient Greek οὐ (ou, “not”) + τόπος (tópos, “place, region”) + -ία (-ía). Compare English topos and -ia.

parole.significato: To clean (something) with a vacuum cleaner.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin vacuum (“vacuum”), a subsense of Classical Latin vacuum (“empty space”), a substantivised form of vacuus (“empty”); related to vacāre (“to be empty”). The exercise sense comes from analogy to the sucking action of a vacuum cleaner.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or affecting the vagina.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin vāgīnālis, from vāgīna (“a covering, sheath; the vagina”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to vagina + -al.

parole.significato: A speech made when leaving or parting company.
parole.testo: First attested in 1614; borrowed from New Latin valedictiō, from valedīcō (“to bid farewell”) + -tiō, from valē (“farewell, so long”) + dīcō (“to say”). By surface analysis, valedict + -ion.

parole.significato: An abode of the gods or afterlife in general.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Old Norse Valhǫll (from valr (“dead warriors”) + hǫll (“hall”)).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to valves, such as those of the heart.
parole.testo: From New Latin valvulāris, from valvula + -āris. By surface analysis, valvula + -ar.

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol V) with atomic number 23; it is a transition metal, used in the production of special steels.
parole.testo: Mid 19th century, from New Latin vanadium.

parole.significato: An acute, highly contagious pathogenic disease caused by the varicella zoster virus, primarily affecting children and c…
parole.testo: From New Latin varicella, diminutive of variola (“pox”).

parole.significato: The duct in the testicle that carries semen from the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct.
parole.testo: From New Latin vās dēferēns, itself from vās (“vessel, duct”) + dēferēns (“carrying off”, present active participle of dēferō (“to carry off”)).

parole.significato: Relating to the flow of fluids, such as blood, lymph, or sap, through the body of an animal or plant, or to the vessels…
parole.testo: From New Latin vasculāris, from Latin vasculum, diminutive of vas (“vessel”).

parole.significato: Vessel: Relating to blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, or both.
parole.testo: From New Latin vasculāris, from Latin vasculum.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a ventricle or ventriculus.
parole.testo: From New Latin *ventricularis, from ventriculus (“belly, stomach, ventricle”), diminutive of venter (“belly, stomach, womb”). Equivalent to ventricle + -ar; See ventricle.

parole.significato: The appearance of new leaves.
parole.testo: From New Latin vernātiō, from Latin vernāre (“to be verdant, to flourish”) + -tiō (“-tion”, suffix forming abstract nouns), from vernus (“springlike”) + -āre (verb-forming suffix), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wósr̥. Equivalent to vernal + -tion.

parole.significato: The formation of vertebrae.
parole.testo: From New Latin vertebrātiō. By surface analysis, vertebra + -ation.

parole.significato: An elevation or crest in the wall of the urethra where the seminal ducts enter it.
parole.testo: From New Latin veru montānum (literally “mountainous javelin”).

parole.significato: A device that vibrates or causes vibration.
parole.testo: From New Latin vibrātor, from Latin vibrō (“to vibrate”). By surface analysis, vibrate + -or.

parole.significato: The quality of understanding or experiencing something vicariously.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin vicārietās and/or vicarious + -ity; compare precarity.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Italian anatomist Guido Guidi (latinized name Vidus Vidius).
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Vidianus. By surface analysis, Vidius + an. Named after Italian surgeon and anatomist Vidus Vidius (1509–1569).

parole.significato: Any of several evergreen shrubs, of the genus Vinca, including the periwinkle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Vinca, a back-formation from Latin pervinca.

parole.significato: Any member of the family Viperidae; a viper.
parole.testo: Originally only capitalized, from New Latin Viperidae (“taxonomic family”), as Vipera + -id.

parole.significato: A type of gland, in flatworms and similar organisms, that secretes yolk.
parole.testo: Derived from New Latin, from vitellus (“yolk”) + -ārium (prefix: place associated with). By surface analysis, vitell- + -arium. See also English vitellus.

parole.significato: A supposed chemical element, afterward found to be a mixture of several metals, such as copper, iron, lead, nickel, etc.
parole.testo: From New Latin.

parole.significato: blood volume
parole.testo: From volume + -emia (-emia is from New Latin).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to birds.
parole.testo: From New Latin volucrinus, from Latin volucer.

parole.significato: Repeated ineffectual attempts at vomiting; retching.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin vomitūritiō (“nausea”), alteration of vomitiō (“a vomiting”).

parole.significato: A fraction written in the form of one integer divided by another, non-zero, integer, e.g. ½.
parole.testo: Calque of New Latin fractiō vulgāris, from Latin vulgāris (“common”), originally in contrast to specialised forms such as “astronomical” (sexagesimal) fractions.

parole.significato: A mixture of a powdered mineral substance (often slaked lime (containing calcium hydroxide), chalk (calcium carbonate),…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from white (adjective) + wash (noun). Noun sense 5.1 (“medicinal preparation for treating skin diseases”) is a calque of New Latin lōtiō alba (literally “white wash”). The verb is derived partly from white (adjective) + wash (verb), and partly from the noun.

parole.significato: The chemical element wolfram or tungsten.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin wolframium.

parole.significato: A deposit of cholesterol on the eyelid.
parole.testo: From New Latin xanthelasma, from Ancient Greek ξανθός (xanthós, “yellow”) + ἔλασμα (élasma, “metal plate, foil”).

parole.significato: The concept of hospitality to strangers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin xenia, from Ancient Greek ξενῐ́ᾱ (xenĭ́ā, “hospitality”).

parole.significato: A yellow crystalline carotenoid alcohol that occurs widely with lutein, with which it is isomeric, and is the chief pig…
parole.testo: From New Latin Zea (genus name of Indian corn) + xanthin.

parole.significato: One who believed that maize was the cause of pellagra.
parole.testo: From New Latin zea, from Ancient Greek ζειά (zeiá, “spelt”), + -ist.

parole.significato: A kind of tree in the elm family (genus Zelkova).
parole.testo: From New Latin (genus name) from Russian дзе́льква (dzélʹkva, “tree, wood”), from Georgian ძელქვა (ʒelkva), from Old Georgian ძელქვაჲ (ʒelkvay), from ძელი (ʒeli, “beam”) + ქვაჲ (kvay, “stone”).

parole.significato: A zenaida dove (Zenaida spp.).
parole.testo: From the New Latin genus name Zenaida.

parole.significato: relating to the square of a number
parole.testo: From New Latin zenzicus, zensicus, from zensus, Germanized from census / German zenzi (“square (of a number)”), from Italian censo (“property”), used in Medieval times to denote the algebraic square based on a translation of Arabic مَال (māl, “property, assets, estate; (obsolete) algebraic square”).

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Zieria.
parole.testo: From the New Latin genus name Zieria.

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol Zr) with an atomic number of 40, a strong, lustrous, grey-white transition metal mainly used…
parole.testo: From a New Latin coinage, from zircon. Doublet of jargonium.

parole.significato: One of the cells or tubes which enclose the feeding zooids of Bryozoa.
parole.testo: From New Latin zōoecium, from Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”) + οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).

parole.significato: zoology
parole.testo: From New Latin zōognōsia. By surface analysis, zoo- + -gnosy.

parole.significato: A distinct organism.
parole.testo: First adopted by Herbert Spencer in Principles of Biology (see 1864 quotation): from New Latin zōon, from Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).

parole.significato: The dissection or anatomy of animals.
parole.testo: From New Latin zōotomia, corresponding to zoo- + -tomy.

parole.significato: A larval stage of certain decapod crustaceans, especially of decapods such as crabs and certain Anomura, also called th…
parole.testo: From New Latin zōaea, zōēa, from Ancient Greek ζωή (zōḗ, “life”) (compare ζῷον (zōîon)).

parole.significato: One of several small subcutaneous facial muscles arising from or in relation with the zygomatic bone.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from New Latin zygomaticus, clipping of mūsculus zygomaticus (“zygomatic muscle”). Doublet of zygomatic.

parole.significato: A slender band of muscle on each side of the face that arises from the zygomatic bone, inserts into the orbicularis ori…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin zygomaticus major, clipping of mūsculus zygomaticus major (“larger zygomatic muscle”).

parole.significato: A slender band of muscle on each side of the face that arises from the zygomatic bone, inserts into the upper lip betwe…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin zygomaticus minor, clipping of mūsculus zygomaticus minor (“smaller zygomatic muscle”).

parole.significato: The act of uniting by glue or other tenacious substance; the state of being thus united; adhesion of parts.
parole.testo: Multiple origins. The oldest usage, in relation to tissues adhering or healing in medical contexts, appears in the 16th century, from French agglutination. The linguistic sense derived from this usage during the early 19th century. The sense of gluing or cementing objects together in other contexts

parole.significato: Any large nonvenomous snake of the genus Eunectes, found mainly in northern South America.
parole.testo: From New Latin anacandaia (“python”), originally referring to a species of constrictor found in Sri Lanka, from Sinhalese හෙනකඳයා (henakaⁿdayā, “whip snake”), from හෙණ (heṇa, “lightning, thunderbolt”) + කඳ (kaⁿda, “stem, trunk, body”) or from Tamil ஆனைக்கொன்றான் (āṉaikkoṉṟāṉ, “having killed an eleph

parole.significato: Any amphibian of the order Anura: any frog (narrow sense) or toad.
parole.testo: From New Latin Anoura, Anura (“name of the order of amphibians”), or from French Anoures (“name of a family of amphibians”), from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-, “lacking”)) + Ancient Greek οὐρά (ourá, “tail”) + -an.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or located at a base, but especially at the base of the skull or an organ of Corti.
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin basilāris, irregularly from basis (“a pedestal, foot, base”) + -āris (“-ar, -ary”, adjectival suffix); or from French basilaire, from base (“base, basis”) + -aire (“-ar, -ary”, adjectival suffix), in the pattern of cimbalaire (“cymbal-shaped”).

parole.significato: To bring to, or direct toward, a common center; to unite more closely; to gather into one body, mass, or force.
parole.testo: (early 17th century) From a Romance language, see French concentrer, Italian concentràre, Spanish concentrar; alternatively from Medieval Latin/New Latin concentrō + -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare also earlier concentre and German konzentrieren. By surface analysis, con- + center (centr- in com

parole.significato: Having the form of a wedge; wedge-shaped, especially with a tapered end.
parole.testo: From French cunéiforme or New Latin cuneifōrmis, from Classical Latin cuneus (“wedge”) + fōrma.

parole.significato: (obsolete) niobium (although formerly thought as a distinct element)
parole.testo: From New Latin dianium, from Latin Diana; either as the name of the Roman goddess, or from its use in Old English as a name of silver.

parole.significato: To fart, to emit digestive gases from the anus, especially with accompanying sound and smell.
parole.testo: Attested since the 19th century; either a back-formation from flatulence or borrowed from French flatuler, either way, see-ate (verb-forming suffix); ultimately from New Latin flātulentus, from flō (“to blow, breeze”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, originating in, characteristic of, or deriving from Muslims or Islam.
parole.testo: From Islam + -ic, probably after New Latin islāmicus or French islamique.

parole.significato: A clear liquid believed to be a component of a humour or other bodily fluid (esp. plasma and lymph).
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin latex (“clear fluid which is part of a humour or bodily fluid”), a later use of Latin latex (“water; liquid, fluid”). parole.significato: Synonym of leprous, afflicted with leprosy.
parole.testo: From New Latin leprōsus in botany especially as used by Linnaeus in his 1753 Species Plantarum and Late Latin leprōsus in medicine, from lepra (“psoriasis, leprosy”) + -ōsus, from Koine Greek λέπρᾱ (léprā, “psoriasis & similar skin diseases”), from Ancient Greek λεπρός (leprós, “scaly”), from either

parole.significato: A type of bolthead flask used in chemical distillation.
parole.testo: From New Latin matracium and its source, Middle French matheras, matraz etc., either from Middle French materas (see Etymology 1, above), with reference to its shape, or from Arabic مطرة, مطارة (“leather bottle, vase”).

parole.significato: The thorax of a crustacean, between the head (cephalon) and abdomen (pleon).
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin, from Ancient Greek περαιόω (peraióō, “to transport”), so called from the location of the legs on the thorax. Alternatively, from περί (perí, “around”) + ἰέναι (iénai, “to go”).

parole.significato: The abdomen of a crustacean.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin, from Ancient Greek πλέων (pléōn), present participle of πλεῖν (pleîn, “to sail”); from the fact that it bears the swimming limbs. Alternatively, perhaps in the sense of being longer or extended.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to, prosody.
parole.testo: From prosody or its etymon Classical Latin prosōdia + -ic, probably after French prosodique, New Latin prosōdicus.
